bio_edx.3.0.summary: **Charles Darwin** and **Alfred Russel Wallace** each gathered evidence on long voyages and **independently** came up with the theory of **evolution by natural selection**. Their ideas were presented together at the **Linnean Society in 1858**, and Darwin published **'On the Origin of Species' in 1859**. Their work replaced the widely held belief that species were **fixed and created** in their present form with the idea that species **change over time** through the selection of inherited variation, although it took many years, and the later discovery of genes, for the theory to be widely accepted.

core.h: Scientific thinking before Darwin and Wallace
core.p: In the early 1800s most people in Britain believed that every species had been **created by God** in its present form and **did not change**. This is called the **creationist** view.
bullets: Species were thought to be **fixed**: the same now as when first created.
The Earth was widely thought to be only a few thousand years old, too young for slow change.
**Fossils** of extinct species were already known and were hard to explain with this view.

**Lamarck** had suggested species change, but by the **inheritance of acquired characteristics** (features gained during life, such as stretched necks, being passed on). This idea was later shown to be wrong.

callouts.p: Darwin and Wallace's theory challenged the idea that species were created and fixed, which is why it was so controversial.

core.p: Charles Darwin was a naturalist on the ship **HMS Beagle**, which sailed around the world from **1831 to 1836**.
bullets: He collected and observed **plants, animals and fossils** in many places, especially South America.
On the **Galapagos Islands** he noticed that **finches** and **tortoises** differed from island to island.
Each type of finch had a **beak suited to the food** available on its island.
He found **fossils** of extinct animals that resembled living species in the same region.
He also studied **variation** in domesticated animals such as pigeons, and how breeders select features.

core.p: Darwin combined his observations with ideas from other scientists to explain them.
bullets: **Charles Lyell** (geologist) argued the Earth was **very old**, giving enough time for slow change.
**Thomas Malthus** wrote that populations produce more offspring than can survive, so there is a **struggle for existence**.
Darwin realised that individuals with useful variations would be **more likely to survive and reproduce**.
He spent about **20 years** gathering more evidence before publishing, partly because he knew the idea would be controversial.

core.p: **Alfred Russel Wallace** was a naturalist who collected specimens in the **Amazon** and then the **Malay Archipelago** (south-east Asia) from 1854 to 1862.
bullets: He collected thousands of specimens and studied how species were **distributed** across islands.
He noticed a boundary between Asian and Australian animals, now called the **Wallace line**.

He studied **warning colouration**: bright colours in some animals (such as caterpillars and butterflies) warn predators they taste bad, which he explained as an **adaptation** produced by natural selection.
In **1858** he **independently** worked out the theory of natural selection and sent an essay describing it to Darwin.
His evidence **supported** Darwin's theory and helped persuade Darwin to publish.

callouts.p: Wallace developed the theory of evolution by natural selection independently of Darwin, at the same time.

core.h: 1858 and 1859: the theory is made public
core.p: Because Wallace and Darwin had reached the same conclusion, their work was presented **together**.
bullets: **1858**: papers by Darwin and Wallace were read at a meeting of the **Linnean Society** in London.
**1859**: Darwin published **'On the Origin of Species'**, setting out the theory and a large amount of evidence.
The book became a best seller and sparked fierce public debate.
Both scientists are credited with the theory, but Darwin is better known because of his detailed book.

core.p: Darwin and Wallace explained evolution as a result of **natural selection** acting on variation. (The detailed steps are a separate spec point.)
bullets: Individuals in a species show **variation**.
More offspring are produced than can survive, so there is **competition**.
Those best adapted are **more likely to survive and reproduce**.
They pass on their characteristics to offspring.
Over many generations the species **changes**; this is **evolution**.

callouts.p: A change in the inherited characteristics of a population over time through a process of natural selection, which may result in the formation of new species.

core.h: How their evidence supported the theory
core.p: Strong theories need evidence. Darwin and Wallace used a wide range of observations.
bullets: **Differences between island species** (finches, tortoises) suggested species had changed to suit local conditions.
**Fossils** showed extinct species similar to living ones, suggesting change over time.
**Selective breeding** showed that selecting variation can change a species over generations.
**Distribution of species** (Wallace's work) matched the idea that species spread and changed in different areas.
**Warning colouration** showed how features useful for survival become common.

core.h: Why the theory was not accepted straight away
core.p: Many people, including scientists, rejected the theory at first. Grade 9 answers give **several reasons**.
bullets: It **challenged religious beliefs** that God created all species, and that humans were created separately.
The suggestion that humans and apes shared a common ancestor upset many people.
There was **not enough evidence** at the time to convince many scientists.
The **mechanism of inheritance was unknown**: nobody knew how variation was passed on, because **genes** had not been discovered.
**Mendel's** work on inheritance (1866) was not recognised until **1900**.

callouts.p: The best answers mention three reasons: religion, insufficient evidence, and no known mechanism of inheritance.

core.p: Over time, more evidence built up and the theory became the **accepted scientific explanation** of how life changes.
bullets: Rediscovery of **Mendel's work** and discovery of **genes and chromosomes** explained how characteristics are inherited.
Discovery of **DNA** and **mutations** explained where new variation comes from.
More **fossils** were found, showing gradual change.
Evolution has been **observed directly**, for example antibiotic resistance in bacteria.
Combining natural selection with genetics gave the modern theory of evolution.

core.p: Darwin and Wallace's work **changed how scientists think** about living things, not just one fact.
bullets: Species are **not fixed**; they **change over time** and new species can form.
All living things are related and share **common ancestors**.
Humans are part of the natural world and evolved like other species.
It gave biology a **unifying explanation** for adaptation, diversity and extinction.
It replaced **Lamarck's** idea of inheritance of acquired characteristics.
It led to new research areas, such as **classification** based on evolutionary relationships.

core.p: Exam questions often ask you to contrast the two explanations, using a giraffe's neck as an example.
bullets: **Lamarck**: giraffes stretched their necks to reach leaves; the longer neck gained in life was passed on.
**Darwin and Wallace**: giraffes already **varied** in neck length; those with longer necks got more food, survived and reproduced more, passing on the **inherited** long-neck characteristic.
Lamarck's idea is wrong because changes gained during life (such as muscles from exercise) are **not inherited**.

callouts.p: Do not write that organisms change because they 'need' to or 'try' to. Variation already exists; the environment selects it.

analogy.t: Two detectives cracking the same case
analogy.p: Imagine two detectives working on opposite sides of the world. One (Darwin) has spent 20 years collecting clues from islands, fossils and pigeon breeders; the other (Wallace) has been gathering clues in the jungles of south-east Asia. Without talking, both reach the same culprit: natural selection. When Wallace posts his solution to Darwin, they announce it together, and Darwin publishes the full case file. The town (society) at first refuses to believe it because it contradicts what everyone was taught, and the detectives cannot yet explain exactly how the culprit operated (genes). Later forensic science (genetics, DNA) confirms the solution. The analogy breaks down because in science a theory is never closed like a court case; it stays open to new evidence and has been refined since.

mistakes.r: Wallace independently proposed the same theory; their papers were presented together in 1858.

mistakes.w: People rejected Darwin because he had no evidence.
mistakes.r: He had a lot of evidence, but there was not enough to convince many, it challenged religious beliefs, and the mechanism of inheritance (genes) was unknown.

mistakes.r: Finches varied in beak shape; those with beaks suited to the food survived and reproduced, passing on the characteristic.

mistakes.r: Evolution is a change in the inherited characteristics of a population over many generations.

exam.q: Name the scientist who independently developed the theory of evolution by natural selection at the same time as Darwin.
model: Alfred Russel Wallace.
exam.tip: Spell Wallace correctly.

exam.q: Give the title of the book Darwin published in 1859.
model: On the Origin of Species.
exam.tip: 'Origin of Species' is accepted.

exam.q: State one observation Darwin made on the Galapagos Islands.
model: Finches / tortoises on different islands had different features, e.g. beak shapes suited to their food.
exam.tip: Give a specific observation.

exam.q: Describe one piece of work by Wallace that supported the theory of natural selection.
model: Studied warning colouration in animals (e.g. butterflies / caterpillars).
Explained bright colours as an adaptation that helped survival, so selected for / OR studied distribution of species across the Malay Archipelago showing species varied between regions.
exam.tip: Name the work and link it to natural selection.

exam.q: Suggest why Darwin waited many years before publishing his theory.
model: He knew the theory would be controversial / challenge religious beliefs.
He wanted to collect more evidence to support it.
exam.tip: Two different reasons.

exam.q: Explain why the theory of evolution by natural selection was not accepted by many people when it was first published.
model: It challenged the religious belief that God created all species / species are fixed.
There was insufficient evidence at the time to convince many scientists.
The mechanism of inheritance / genes was not known.
exam.tip: Three separate reasons for three marks.

exam.q: Compare Lamarck's and Darwin's explanations for giraffes having long necks.
model: Lamarck: giraffes stretched necks during their lifetime.
Lamarck: this acquired characteristic was passed to offspring.
Darwin: giraffes showed variation in neck length; long-necked giraffes reached more food so survived and reproduced.
Darwin: the inherited characteristic was passed on, so over generations necks became longer.
exam.tip: Balance both sides; key difference is acquired vs inherited.

exam.q: Describe how the discovery of genetics helped the theory of natural selection become accepted.
model: Mendel's work / discovery of genes explained how characteristics are inherited.
Mutations / DNA explained how new variation arises.
exam.tip: Link genetics to the missing mechanism.

exam.q: Explain how the work of Darwin and Wallace changed scientific thinking about the origin of species.
model: Before, most people believed species were created by God and fixed.
Darwin and Wallace proposed species change over time by natural selection.
This suggested all species share common ancestors / humans evolved like other species.
It replaced Lamarck's ideas and became the accepted explanation once supported by genetics and further evidence.
exam.tip: Show the before and after.

exam.q: Evaluate the contributions of Darwin and Wallace to the theory of evolution by natural selection.
model: Darwin: Beagle voyage, observations of Galapagos finches / tortoises and fossils.
Darwin: studied selective breeding; spent around 20 years collecting evidence; published Origin of Species (1859) with large amount of evidence.
Wallace: worked in Amazon and Malay Archipelago; studied species distribution and warning colouration.
Wallace: independently reached the same theory; his 1858 essay led to joint presentation at the Linnean Society and spurred Darwin to publish.
Both changed thinking from fixed, created species to species changing over time.
Judgement: Darwin gave the most detailed evidence, but Wallace's independent discovery strengthened the theory and both deserve credit.
exam.tip: Describe both, then make a reasoned judgement.

worked.q: Model answer: explain how Darwin's observations of Galapagos finches support evolution by natural selection.
steps: Finches on different islands had different beak shapes.
Each beak shape suited the main food on that island (seeds, insects).
Darwin suggested the finches came from a common ancestor from the mainland.
On each island, birds with beaks suited to the local food survived and reproduced more.
Over many generations each population changed, producing different species.
worked.ans: Different, well-adapted beaks on different islands are explained by natural selection acting on variation in a common ancestor.

worked.q: Applied example: a student says 'Darwin's theory was rejected because it was wrong.' Correct this statement.
steps: The theory was rejected by many at first, not because it was wrong.
It challenged religious beliefs that species were created and fixed.
There was limited evidence and no known mechanism of inheritance.
Later discoveries of genes, DNA and more fossils supported it.
worked.ans: It was rejected because of religious objections, limited evidence and no known mechanism, but later evidence showed it was correct and it is now accepted.

worked.q: Applied example: explain how Wallace would account for a brightly coloured caterpillar that tastes bad to birds.
steps: Caterpillars varied in colour.
Birds learned to avoid bright, bad-tasting caterpillars.
Bright caterpillars were more likely to survive and reproduce.
They passed on the alleles for bright colour, so the colour became more common.
worked.ans: Warning colouration is an adaptation produced by natural selection because it reduces predation.

bio_edx.3.1.summary: Darwin's theory of evolution by natural selection explains how species change over many generations. Individuals in a population show **genetic variation** (originally caused by **mutation**); those with characteristics best suited to the environment are more likely to **survive and reproduce**, so they pass on their **advantageous alleles**. Over many generations the frequency of these alleles increases in the population, which can eventually lead to new species.

core.p: **Evolution** is the gradual change in the inherited characteristics of a population over time. Darwin proposed that the mechanism driving this change is **natural selection**: the environment 'selects' which individuals survive long enough to breed.
bullets: Evolution happens to **populations**, not to individuals during their lifetime.
Changes are **inherited**: they are carried in **genes / alleles** passed on in gametes.
It usually takes **many generations**, so it is slow in large animals and fast in organisms that reproduce quickly (bacteria).
Over very long periods evolution can produce **new species** from an ancestral species.

callouts.p: A change in the inherited characteristics of a population over time through a process of natural selection, which may result in the formation of new species.

core.p: Members of the same species are not identical. Some of this variation is **genetic** (caused by differences in alleles) and some is environmental. Only genetic variation can be passed on, so only genetic variation matters for natural selection.
bullets: Genetic variation arises from **mutations** (changes in the DNA base sequence) which create **new alleles**.
Sexual reproduction (meiosis and random fertilisation) shuffles existing alleles into new combinations.
Most mutations have **no effect** on phenotype; a few are harmful; **rarely** a mutation gives an advantage.
An advantageous mutation is present **before** the environment changes: organisms do not mutate 'because they need to'.

callouts.p: New alleles come from mutation. Without genetic variation there is nothing for natural selection to act on.

core.p: Darwin noticed that organisms produce **more offspring than the environment can support**. Resources are limited, so individuals must **compete** with each other.
bullets: Competition for **food, water, space / territory, light (plants) and mates**.
Individuals also face **predators, disease (pathogens)** and changes in climate.
Population sizes stay roughly stable because many offspring die before reproducing.
This is often summarised as a **struggle for existence**.

core.h: Step 3: Survival of the best adapted
core.p: Individuals with characteristics (phenotypes) that are **best suited to the environment** are more likely to survive the competition. This is what Darwin meant by **survival of the fittest**: 'fittest' means best adapted, not strongest.
bullets: An advantageous characteristic might be better camouflage, faster speed, resistance to a disease, or tolerance of drought.
Less well-adapted individuals are more likely to **die before reproducing**.
What counts as 'advantageous' depends on the **environment**: change the environment and different characteristics are selected.

callouts.p: In exams write 'best adapted to the environment'. 'Fit' and 'strong' alone do not score.

core.p: The survivors **breed**. Because the advantageous characteristic is genetic, they pass the **advantageous allele** on to their offspring in their gametes.
bullets: Surviving is not enough: the key point is that the individual **reproduces** and passes on alleles.
Offspring are therefore more likely to have the advantageous characteristic.
Individuals without the advantage leave **fewer offspring**, so their alleles are passed on less often.

core.p: Repeated over **many generations**, the proportion (frequency) of the advantageous allele in the population **increases** and the disadvantageous allele becomes less common. The population has evolved.
bullets: The characteristic becomes **more common** in the population, not suddenly universal.
If populations become isolated and change in different ways, they may eventually be unable to interbreed to produce fertile offspring: a **new species** has formed.
Species that cannot adapt to a changing environment may become **extinct**.

callouts.p: Variation (mutation) -> competition -> best adapted survive -> reproduce -> pass on advantageous allele -> allele frequency increases over many generations.

core.p: A classic example from industrial Britain. The peppered moth has a pale form and a dark (melanic) form controlled by alleles of one gene. Moths rest on tree bark by day and are eaten by birds.
bullets: Before the Industrial Revolution, bark was pale with lichen, so **pale moths were camouflaged** and dark moths were eaten more.
Soot pollution killed lichens and blackened bark, so **dark moths were now camouflaged**.
Dark moths survived predation by birds more often, reproduced and passed on the dark allele.
Over many generations dark moths became the most common form in polluted areas.
After clean air laws, bark became paler again and pale moths increased again: selection depends on the environment.

core.p: Giraffes are a common exam context because the Darwinian explanation is easily confused with the wrong (Lamarckian) explanation.
bullets: Ancestral giraffes showed **variation** in neck length due to different alleles.
When food was scarce, those with **longer necks could reach higher leaves**, so had more food.
They were more likely to survive, reproduce and pass on the alleles for long necks.
Over many generations average neck length in the population increased.

Wrong idea (Lamarck): giraffes stretched their necks during their lives and passed on the stretched neck. Characteristics acquired during a lifetime are **not inherited** because they do not change the DNA in gametes.

callouts.p: Organisms do not change because they want or need to. Variation already exists; the environment selects it.

core.p: Natural selection can be watched happening in bacteria because they reproduce very rapidly (as often as every 20 minutes). Antibiotic resistance is covered in detail in point 4.3, but it is the clearest modern support for Darwin's theory.
bullets: A random mutation gives one bacterium resistance.
The antibiotic kills non-resistant bacteria; the resistant one survives and multiplies.
The population becomes mostly resistant within a short time.

core.p: Darwin published **On the Origin of Species** in 1859. It was not accepted straight away.
bullets: It challenged the religious idea that God created all species in their present form.
There was **not enough evidence** at the time; few transitional fossils were known.
The **mechanism of inheritance** (genes, Mendel's work) was not known, so Darwin could not explain how variation was passed on.
Today the theory is supported by fossils, DNA comparisons, antibiotic resistance and observed changes in populations.

core.p: Natural selection changes the **proportion** of individuals carrying an allele. Exam questions often give data showing this change over time.
bullets: The advantageous allele rises slowly at first (few carriers), then faster, then levels off as it becomes common.
Quote numbers from the data and describe the trend, then explain it using natural selection.
A larger selection pressure (e.g. more predators) speeds up the change.

analogy.t: A talent show with no judges, only a fixed number of places
analogy.p: Imagine a talent show where only a few contestants can move on each round, decided by the conditions on the night (the environment). Contestants who happen to suit the conditions get through and their 'act' is copied by the next set of contestants (offspring inherit alleles). Over many rounds, the winning style becomes common. It breaks down because in nature nobody is choosing or aiming for a goal, contestants cannot rehearse or improve their act (acquired traits are not inherited), and new styles appear only by random mutation.

terms.d: A change in the inherited characteristics of a population over time through natural selection, which may result in the formation of new species.
The process by which individuals best adapted to their environment are more likely to survive and reproduce, passing on their advantageous alleles.
Differences in characteristics between individuals of the same species.
Variation caused by differences in the alleles individuals inherit.
A change in the base sequence of DNA, which can produce a new allele.
A different version of the same gene.
A characteristic that helps an organism survive and reproduce in its environment.
The struggle between organisms for limited resources such as food, water, space and mates.
Darwin's phrase meaning that the individuals best adapted to the environment are most likely to survive and reproduce.
A factor in the environment, such as predation, disease or competition, that affects which individuals survive.
How common an allele is in a population.
A group of organisms that can interbreed to produce fertile offspring.
When no individuals of a species remain alive.
The passing of genetic information (alleles) from parents to offspring in gametes.

mistakes.w: The giraffe stretched its neck so its babies had long necks.
mistakes.r: Variation in neck length already existed; long-necked giraffes survived, reproduced and passed on the alleles for long necks.

mistakes.w: The organism mutated in order to survive.
mistakes.r: Mutations are random and happen before the selection pressure; the environment then selects individuals that already have the allele.

mistakes.w: The strongest animals survive.
mistakes.r: Individuals best adapted to the environment are more likely to survive.

mistakes.w: The animals survive (and stop there).
mistakes.r: They survive **and reproduce**, passing on the advantageous allele to offspring.

mistakes.w: They pass on the characteristic / the gene for survival.
mistakes.r: They pass on the **advantageous allele** in their gametes.

mistakes.w: The individual evolves during its life.
mistakes.r: The **population** evolves over many generations.

mistakes.w: All the population changes in one generation.
mistakes.r: The allele becomes more frequent over **many generations**.

mistakes.w: Bacteria become used to / immune to the antibiotic.
mistakes.r: A mutation makes some bacteria resistant; they survive and reproduce so the resistant population grows.

exam.q: State what is meant by evolution.
model: A change in the inherited characteristics of a population over time (through natural selection).
exam.tip: Include 'inherited' and 'population'.

exam.q: Name the process that produces new alleles in a population.
model: Mutation.
exam.tip: Not 'variation' - variation is the result.

exam.q: Give two resources that animals in a population may compete for.
model: Food.
Mates / water / space / territory (any one).
exam.tip: Light and minerals are for plants only.

exam.q: Explain why Darwin's theory was not accepted by many scientists when it was first published.
model: Insufficient evidence at the time.
Mechanism of inheritance (genes) was not known / it challenged the belief that God created all species.
exam.tip: Two separate reasons for two marks.

exam.q: Explain why a characteristic that an animal develops during its lifetime, such as large muscles, cannot be passed to its offspring.
model: It does not change the DNA / alleles.
Of the gametes, so it is not inherited.
exam.tip: Link to gametes and DNA.

exam.q: Snowshoe hares in a cold region have white fur in winter. Explain how natural selection could have led to most hares having white winter fur.
model: Variation in fur colour (due to mutation).
Hares with white fur are camouflaged in snow so less likely to be eaten by predators.
These hares survive and reproduce.
Pass on the allele for white fur, which becomes more common over many generations.
exam.tip: Apply each stage to the hare; do not write a generic answer.

exam.q: Describe how a mutation could lead to an increase in a population of an advantageous characteristic.
model: Mutation produces a new allele.
Allele gives an advantage in the environment.
Individuals with it more likely to survive and reproduce.
Allele passed to offspring so its frequency increases over generations.
exam.tip: Start with the mutation and end with frequency.

exam.q: The percentage of dark peppered moths in an industrial city rose from 2% in 1848 to 95% in 1895. Explain this change.
model: Soot from pollution darkened tree bark.
Dark moths were camouflaged so fewer eaten by birds.
Dark moths survived and reproduced, passing on the allele for dark colour.
Over many generations the dark allele became more frequent.
exam.tip: Use the figures: 2% to 95% over 47 years.

exam.q: Explain how Darwin's theory of evolution by natural selection accounts for the long necks of modern giraffes.
model: Ancestral giraffes showed variation in neck length.
Variation caused by different alleles / mutation.
Competition for food (leaves) when food was scarce.
Longer-necked giraffes could reach higher leaves so more likely to survive.
Survivors reproduced and passed on the alleles for long necks.
Over many generations the proportion with long necks increased.
exam.tip: A clear logical sequence is needed for level 3. Never say 'stretched'.

exam.q: A species of beetle lives on an island. A new predatory bird arrives. Suggest and explain how the beetle population could change over time.
model: Variation exists among beetles (e.g. colour, speed, hard shell).
Arising from mutation.
The bird eats beetles that are easy to see / catch.
Beetles with the advantageous characteristic more likely to survive and reproduce.
Pass on the advantageous allele to offspring.
Over many generations the characteristic becomes more common (or the population may become extinct if no variation helps).
exam.tip: Choose a sensible characteristic and stick with it.

worked.q: Rabbits were introduced to Australia and the myxoma virus was released to control them. At first 99% died. Years later most rabbits survived infection. Use natural selection to explain this.
steps: Identify variation: a few rabbits carried alleles giving resistance to the virus (from mutation).
Identify the selection pressure: the myxoma virus killed non-resistant rabbits.
Selection: resistant rabbits were more likely to survive.
Reproduction: they bred and passed on the resistance allele.
Outcome: over many generations the proportion of resistant rabbits increased.
worked.ans: Resistant rabbits survived the virus, reproduced and passed on the resistance allele, so over many generations most of the population became resistant.

worked.q: In a population of 200 lizards, 30 have a darker skin that camouflages them on dark rocks. After several generations, 150 out of 250 lizards are dark. Calculate the percentage of dark lizards before and after, and explain the change.
steps: Increase of 45 percentage points.
Explanation: dark lizards were camouflaged so fewer were eaten by predators; they survived, reproduced and passed on the allele for dark skin.
worked.ans: 15% rising to 60%, because natural selection favoured the camouflaged dark lizards.

worked.q: A student writes: 'Cheetahs needed to run faster to catch prey, so they evolved longer legs.' Rewrite this to gain full marks.
steps: Remove the idea of need or trying.
Start with variation: ancestral cheetahs varied in speed due to different alleles.
Faster cheetahs caught more prey so were more likely to survive.
They reproduced and passed on the alleles for speed / long legs.
Over many generations the population became faster on average.
worked.ans: Ancestral cheetahs showed variation in speed; the fastest caught more food, survived, reproduced and passed on their alleles, so over many generations cheetahs became faster.

bio_edx.3.10.summary: Farmers need to grow more food on the same land for a growing world population. **Fertilisers** put back the mineral ions (especially nitrates, phosphates and potassium) that crops take from the soil, so plants can make more protein, chlorophyll and new cells and give higher yields. **Biological control** uses a natural predator, parasite or pathogen of a pest to keep its numbers down, reducing crop losses without chemical pesticides. Both raise yields, but both have costs and risks that you must be able to evaluate.

core.h: Why we need to increase food yields
core.p: The world population keeps rising, so we need more food without clearing ever more land. **Food security** means everyone having access to enough safe, nutritious food. Yield can be raised by giving crops what they need to grow (fertilisers) and by stopping pests eating or damaging them (pest control).
bullets: **Crop yield** = the mass of useful crop produced per unit area of land (for example tonnes per hectare).
Yield is reduced by a shortage of **mineral ions** in the soil, by **pests** (insects, slugs, weeds) and by disease.
Increasing yield on existing farmland reduces the need to destroy habitats such as forests.
The two methods in this spec point: **fertilisers** and **biological control**.

callouts.p: The amount of crop (mass of useful product) harvested from a given area of land.

core.p: Plants make glucose by photosynthesis, but to turn glucose into proteins, DNA and chlorophyll they also need **mineral ions**, which they absorb from soil water through their **root hair cells** by **active transport**.
bullets: **Nitrates** supply nitrogen to make **amino acids and proteins**, needed for growth. Shortage: stunted growth, yellow older leaves.
**Phosphates** supply phosphorus for **DNA**, **ATP** and cell membranes. Shortage: poor root growth, purple leaves.
**Potassium** ions help **enzymes** for photosynthesis and respiration work. Shortage: yellow leaves with dead patches.
**Magnesium** ions are needed to make **chlorophyll**. Shortage: yellow leaves (chlorosis).
Without these ions a plant cannot grow well even if it has plenty of light, water and carbon dioxide.

head: Mineral ion
Used for
Deficiency symptom
rows: Poor root growth, purple younger leaves

callouts.p: Most fertilisers are labelled NPK: nitrogen (as nitrate or ammonium), phosphorus (as phosphate) and potassium.

core.h: Why soils run short of minerals
core.p: In a natural ecosystem, plants die and are **decomposed**, so their mineral ions return to the soil. On a farm the crop is **harvested and removed**, so the minerals it absorbed are taken away and the cycle is broken.
bullets: Each harvest removes nitrogen, phosphorus and potassium locked up in the crop.
Growing the same crop year after year drains the same ions.
Rain can **leach** soluble ions such as nitrates down out of reach of roots.
So farmers must **replace** the lost mineral ions or yields fall.

callouts.p: If asked why fertilisers are needed, say minerals are removed when the crop is harvested so they are not returned to the soil by decay.

core.p: A **fertiliser** is a substance added to soil to supply mineral ions that increase plant growth. There are two main types.
bullets: **Artificial (chemical) fertilisers** are made in factories, for example ammonium nitrate. They contain known amounts of specific ions and dissolve quickly.
**Natural (organic) fertilisers** include **manure** and **compost**. Decomposers break them down slowly to release mineral ions.
Artificial fertilisers can be matched exactly to what the crop needs.
Natural fertilisers also add **organic matter (humus)**, improving soil structure and water retention, and recycle farm waste.

head: Feature
Artificial fertiliser
Natural fertiliser (manure, compost)
rows: Slow, as decomposers break it down
Must be bought, energy used to make

callouts.p: A substance added to soil to provide mineral ions, such as nitrates, phosphates and potassium, needed for plant growth.

core.p: Fertilisers raise yield because they remove a **limiting factor** for growth. More nitrate means more amino acids, so more **protein** for new cells; more magnesium means more chlorophyll, so more photosynthesis.
bullets: More nitrate gives more protein, so **faster growth** and bigger plants.
More chlorophyll means more light is absorbed, so **more photosynthesis** and more glucose.
More glucose can be used for respiration (energy for growth) and stored as starch, increasing the useful crop.
Healthier plants may be better at resisting disease.
Result: **higher crop yield** from the same area of land.

callouts.p: Fertiliser adds nitrate, plant makes more amino acids and proteins, more cell growth, higher yield.

core.h: Using the right amount of fertiliser
core.p: Adding fertiliser only helps while minerals are the **limiting factor**. Once something else (light, water, CO2, temperature) limits growth, extra fertiliser gives no extra yield and is wasted money.
bullets: Yield rises steeply at first, then levels off (**plateau**).
Beyond the plateau extra fertiliser is **wasted** and more is likely to run off or leach into water.
Very high concentrations of ions in soil water can lower the water potential around roots, so roots lose water by **osmosis** and plants can wilt.
Good practice: test the soil, apply the right amount at the right time, avoid spreading before heavy rain.

callouts.p: Do not say yield keeps rising with more fertiliser. Describe the plateau and explain it with a different limiting factor.

core.p: If fertiliser is washed by rain from fields into rivers and lakes (**run-off** or **leaching**), it causes **eutrophication**, which can kill fish and other aquatic animals.
bullets: Nitrates and phosphates enter the water.
**Algae** grow rapidly and form an **algal bloom** on the surface.
The bloom **blocks light** from plants below, so they cannot photosynthesise and die.
Algae also die; **decomposer bacteria** break down the dead matter and **respire aerobically**, using up dissolved **oxygen**.
Oxygen levels fall so fish and other animals **die**, and biodiversity falls.
Also: nitrates in drinking water may be a health risk, and fertilisers cost money and energy to make.

callouts.p: Keep the steps in order: fertiliser run-off, algal bloom, light blocked, plants die, bacteria decompose and use oxygen, fish die.
It is the decomposing bacteria respiring that use up the oxygen, not the algae alone.

core.p: **Pests** are organisms that damage crops or compete with them, such as aphids, caterpillars, slugs and weeds. Farmers often use **chemical pesticides** (insecticides, herbicides, fungicides) to kill them.
bullets: Pesticides work quickly and are easy to apply.
They may kill **non-target species**, including useful insects such as bees and natural predators of the pest.
Some are **persistent**: they do not break down and can **bioaccumulate** up food chains, reaching toxic levels in top predators.
Pests can evolve **resistance**, by natural selection, so the pesticide stops working.
Residues may remain on food and must be washed off.
Pesticides must be reapplied, costing money each season.

callouts.p: An organism that reduces crop yield, for example by eating crops, spreading disease or competing for resources.

core.p: **Biological control** is the use of a living organism, such as a **predator**, **parasite** or **pathogen**, to reduce the population of a pest. It is an alternative to chemical pesticides.
bullets: **Ladybirds** are released to eat **aphids** on crops.
The parasitic wasp **Encarsia** lays eggs in **whitefly** larvae in greenhouses; the larvae are killed as the wasp develops.
Some **bacteria and viruses** that infect only certain insect larvae are used to control caterpillars.
Aim: keep the pest population **below the level that causes economic damage**, not to wipe it out completely.
If the control organism wiped out the pest it would then starve, so the two populations settle at a balance.

callouts.p: Using a natural predator, parasite or pathogen of a pest species to reduce the pest population.

core.p: Biological control is often more **specific** and longer lasting than chemical pesticides.
bullets: Often targets **only the pest**, so useful species are not harmed.
No toxic chemicals, so no **bioaccumulation** in food chains and no residues on food.
The pest is unlikely to become **resistant** to being eaten.
The control organism can **reproduce**, so it may not need reapplying, making it cheaper in the long term.
Suitable for **organic farming**.

callouts.p: Biological control works especially well in enclosed greenhouses, where the control organism cannot escape.

core.p: Introducing a new species is risky because ecosystems are complicated and hard to predict.
bullets: **Slower** than pesticides: the pest population falls gradually.
Does not get rid of the pest **completely**.
The control organism may **eat other species** instead of the pest, or become a pest itself.
It may **spread** beyond the farm and disrupt food chains.
It may die out if conditions are unsuitable.
Example: **cane toads** were brought to Australia to eat cane beetles in sugar cane, but they ate many other animals, are poisonous to native predators, and spread rapidly, becoming a serious pest.

callouts.p: A classic example of biological control going wrong. Use it to support a disadvantage in evaluation questions.

core.p: Exam questions often ask you to compare or evaluate the two methods. Give points on both sides.
bullets: Speed: pesticides fast; biological control slow.
Specificity: biological control usually specific; many pesticides are not.
Long term: biological control can be self-sustaining; pesticides need reapplying.
Risk: pesticides risk bioaccumulation and resistance; biological control risks unpredictable effects on the ecosystem.

core.p: An **evaluate** question needs advantages, disadvantages and a **justified conclusion**. Real farms often combine methods, for example applying fertiliser carefully and using **integrated pest management**, where biological control is used first and pesticides only when necessary.
bullets: Weigh up higher yield and food security against environmental damage.
Consider cost, speed, the size of the farm and whether it is open field or greenhouse.
Use data from the question: quote yields or pest numbers with units.
End with a conclusion that follows from your points, for example biological control is better in a greenhouse because the organism cannot escape.

callouts.p: Without a judgement at the end you cannot reach the top band in a 6-mark evaluate question.

analogy.t: Fertiliser as a shopping trip, biological control as a security guard
analogy.p: Think of the soil as a kitchen cupboard. Each harvest carries food out of the house, so the cupboard empties; fertiliser is the shopping trip that restocks the missing ingredients (nitrates for protein, magnesium for chlorophyll). Buying more than you can cook just wastes money and it goes off, like extra fertiliser that leaches into rivers. Biological control is hiring a security guard (ladybirds) to keep out burglars (aphids) instead of spraying the house with poison. Where it breaks down: a real guard can be told what to do, but a control organism makes its own choices, may leave or attack the wrong target (cane toads), and plants do not take minerals from a single store but absorb ions dissolved in soil water by active transport.

terms.d: The mass of useful crop harvested per unit area of land.
Having reliable access to enough safe, nutritious food.
Inorganic ions such as nitrate, phosphate, potassium and magnesium absorbed from the soil and needed for plant growth.
A mineral ion supplying nitrogen, used by plants to make amino acids and proteins.
A mineral ion supplying phosphorus, used to make DNA, ATP and cell membranes.
A substance added to soil to supply mineral ions that increase plant growth.
A manufactured fertiliser containing known amounts of soluble mineral ions, often NPK.
Organic material such as manure or compost that releases mineral ions slowly as it decomposes.
The factor in shortest supply that restricts the rate of a process such as growth or photosynthesis.
Soluble mineral ions being washed through or out of the soil by rainwater.
Excess nutrients in water causing algal growth, then decomposition that removes oxygen and kills aquatic animals.
A rapid increase in algae that covers the surface of water and blocks light.
An organism that reduces crop yield by eating, damaging, infecting or competing with crops.
A chemical used to kill pests, such as an insecticide, herbicide or fungicide.
The build-up of a persistent chemical in organisms, increasing in concentration up a food chain.
Using a natural predator, parasite or pathogen of a pest to reduce the pest population.
Combining methods, mainly biological control, with pesticides used only when needed.

mistakes.w: Fertilisers give plants food or energy.
mistakes.r: Fertilisers supply mineral ions such as nitrates; plants make their own food by photosynthesis.

mistakes.w: Nitrates are used to make glucose.
mistakes.r: Nitrates provide nitrogen to make amino acids and proteins for growth.

mistakes.w: The more fertiliser you add, the higher the yield.
mistakes.r: Yield levels off when another factor such as light becomes limiting; extra fertiliser is wasted and may cause eutrophication.

mistakes.w: In eutrophication the algae use up all the oxygen.
mistakes.r: Bacteria decomposing dead plants and algae respire aerobically and use up the dissolved oxygen.

mistakes.w: Fish die because the fertiliser poisons them.
mistakes.r: Fish die because the oxygen concentration in the water falls.

mistakes.w: Biological control kills all the pests.
mistakes.r: It reduces the pest population to a low level; if all pests died the control organism would starve.

mistakes.w: Biological control has no disadvantages because it is natural.
mistakes.r: The organism may eat other species, spread and become a pest itself, as cane toads did in Australia; it is also slow.

mistakes.w: Pests become resistant to biological control just like pesticides.
mistakes.r: Resistance to a predator is unlikely; resistance is a major problem with chemical pesticides.

mistakes.w: Fertilisers are needed because plants use up the soil.
mistakes.r: Minerals are removed from the field when the crop is harvested, so they are not returned by decomposition.

exam.q: Name the mineral ion plants need to make proteins.
model: Nitrate (ions).
exam.tip: Nitrogen alone is accepted by some mark schemes, but nitrate is safest.

exam.q: Explain why farmers need to add fertiliser to fields that are used to grow crops every year.
model: Crops absorb mineral ions (such as nitrates) from the soil.
The crop is harvested and removed so the minerals are not returned by decay.
exam.tip: The key idea is the cycle being broken by harvesting.

exam.q: Explain how adding nitrate fertiliser increases the yield of a wheat crop.
model: Nitrate is used to make amino acids/proteins.
Proteins are needed for growth of new cells.
So plants grow larger/faster, giving more grain (higher yield).
exam.tip: Link each step: nitrate, protein, growth, yield.

exam.q: Give one advantage of using manure instead of artificial fertiliser.
model: Any one: cheaper/recycles farm waste; adds organic matter and improves soil structure; releases minerals slowly so less leaching.
exam.tip: One clear point is enough for 1 mark.

exam.q: A graph shows that wheat yield increases as fertiliser increases up to 150 kg per hectare and then stays the same. Explain why the yield stops increasing.
model: Mineral ions are no longer the limiting factor.
Another factor, such as light intensity, carbon dioxide, water or temperature, is limiting growth.
exam.tip: Always name a possible alternative limiting factor.

exam.q: Describe what is meant by biological control.
model: Using a living organism / predator / parasite / pathogen.
To reduce the population of a pest.
exam.tip: Make sure you say it is a living organism that is introduced.

exam.q: Parasitic wasps are used to control whitefly in greenhouses. Suggest why biological control is more successful in a greenhouse than in an open field.
model: The wasps cannot escape / are kept with the pest.
So they will not affect other species or ecosystems outside, and their numbers stay high enough to control the pest.
exam.tip: Think about containment.

exam.q: Give two disadvantages of using chemical pesticides.
model: Kill non-target / useful species such as bees or predators.
Pests may become resistant.
Can bioaccumulate in food chains / pollute water / leave residues on food (any two).
exam.tip: Give two different ideas, not two versions of the same one.

exam.q: Explain how fertiliser running off farmland can lead to the death of fish in a lake.
model: Nitrates/phosphates are washed (leach/run off) into the lake.
Algae grow rapidly forming an algal bloom.
The bloom blocks light from reaching plants below the surface.
Plants cannot photosynthesise and die (algae also die).
Bacteria decompose the dead organisms.
Bacteria respire aerobically, using up dissolved oxygen.
Oxygen concentration falls so fish die (any six).
exam.tip: Write it as a numbered chain so no step is missed.

exam.q: Evaluate the use of biological control compared with chemical pesticides to protect crops from insect pests.
model: Biological control is usually specific so does not harm other species.
No chemicals so no bioaccumulation or residues on food.
Pests unlikely to become resistant; control organism reproduces so may not need reapplying.
But it is slower to act and does not remove all pests.
The control organism may eat other species, spread or become a pest (for example cane toads).
Pesticides act quickly but can kill useful insects and pests can evolve resistance.
Conclusion: biological control is better for long-term, contained use such as greenhouses; pesticides may be needed for a sudden outbreak.
exam.tip: Balanced points plus a justified conclusion are needed for the top level.

exam.q: Cane toads were introduced to Australia to control beetles in sugar cane crops. Explain why this is an example of biological control that went wrong.
model: Cane toads ate other native species instead of / as well as the beetles.
They had no natural predators and are poisonous to native predators that eat them.
Their population increased and spread so they became a pest themselves.
exam.tip: Link to the disadvantage that the control organism can become a pest.

worked.q: A farmer adds fertiliser to a field. Yield without fertiliser is 4.0 tonnes per hectare and with fertiliser is 6.5 tonnes per hectare. Calculate the percentage increase in yield.
steps: Increase = 6.5 - 4.0 = 2.5 tonnes per hectare.
Percentage increase = (increase / original) x 100.
worked.ans: 62.5% increase.

worked.q: Whitefly numbers in a greenhouse were 800 per plant before Encarsia wasps were released and 120 per plant after six weeks. Calculate the percentage decrease and explain why the number did not fall to zero.
steps: Percentage decrease = (680 / 800) x 100 = 85%.
As whitefly become scarce, wasps find fewer hosts to lay eggs in, so the wasp population stops increasing.
The two populations reach a balance with the pest kept at a low level.
worked.ans: 85% decrease; biological control keeps the pest low but does not wipe it out, as the wasps depend on the whitefly to reproduce.

worked.q: Model answer: Suggest two reasons why an organic farmer might choose manure and ladybirds rather than artificial fertiliser and insecticide.
steps: Manure is cheap or free on a farm and adds organic matter that improves soil structure.
Manure releases ions slowly so less leaching and less risk of eutrophication.
Ladybirds only eat insects such as aphids, so bees and other useful species are not harmed.
No chemical residues on the food and no bioaccumulation in food chains.
worked.ans: Any two of: cheaper/recycles waste, improves soil, less leaching and eutrophication, no harm to non-target species, no chemical residues or bioaccumulation.

bio_edx.3.11.summary: Selective breeding and genetic engineering both change the genes of organisms to give characteristics that humans want, such as higher crop yields, disease resistance or the production of medicines like human insulin. Both bring big benefits to agriculture and medicine, but both carry risks, such as reduced genetic variation, inbreeding, harm to wildlife and unknown long-term effects. You must be able to weigh up the benefits, risks, practical issues and ethical arguments and reach a justified conclusion.

core.p: **Selective breeding** (artificial selection) is choosing parents with desired characteristics and breeding them over many generations. **Genetic engineering** is changing the genome of an organism by inserting a gene, often from a different species, to give a desired characteristic.
bullets: Selective breeding only mixes alleles that **already exist** in the species.
Genetic engineering can add a gene **from another species**, for example a bacterial gene into a plant.
Selective breeding takes **many generations** (years); genetic engineering can produce the characteristic in **one generation**.
Both are used in **agriculture** (crops and livestock) and genetic engineering is also used in **medicine**.

head: Feature
Selective breeding
Genetic engineering
rows: Many genes passed on, including unwanted ones

callouts.p: Modifying the genome of an organism by introducing a gene from another organism to give a desired characteristic.
Humans choosing organisms with desired characteristics and breeding them together over many generations.

core.p: Selective breeding has produced almost all of the food plants and farm animals we use today.
bullets: Crops with **higher yields**, for example modern wheat with more and larger grains.
Crops with **disease resistance**, so fewer are lost and less pesticide or fungicide is needed.
Dairy cows that produce **more milk**; beef cattle with **more meat**.
Animals that are **gentler (docile)** and easier to handle.
Plants with bigger, sweeter or more attractive fruit and flowers.
Uses no special technology, so it is available to farmers everywhere.

callouts.p: More food from the same land and animals, helping to feed a growing population.

core.p: Breeding only from a few chosen individuals **reduces genetic variation** in the population. This is the root of most of the risks.
bullets: **Inbreeding**: breeding closely related individuals increases the chance of inheriting two copies of a harmful recessive allele, causing **genetic disorders**.
Reduced variation means if a **new disease** appears, there may be no individuals with resistance alleles, so the whole crop or herd could be wiped out.
Less ability to adapt if the **environment changes**.
**Animal health and welfare problems**: some dog breeds have breathing problems or hip problems; fast-growing broiler chickens can have leg problems; very high milk yields can strain dairy cows.
Useful alleles from wild types may be **lost** from the population.

callouts.p: Say selective breeding reduces genetic variation (or reduces the gene pool). Do not say it causes mutations.

core.h: Benefits of genetic engineering in agriculture
core.p: GM crops can be given characteristics that would be impossible or very slow to get by selective breeding.
bullets: **Insect-resistant crops** (Bt crops) make a toxin from the bacterium Bacillus thuringiensis that kills insect pests, so **less insecticide** is sprayed and yields rise.
**Herbicide-resistant crops** let farmers spray weedkiller that kills weeds but not the crop, reducing competition.
**Golden rice** contains genes for making beta-carotene, which the body converts to **vitamin A**, to reduce vitamin A deficiency (which can cause blindness).
Crops tolerant of **drought** or poor soils could be grown in new areas.
Overall: **higher yields** and improved nutrition.

callouts.p: Rice engineered to produce beta-carotene in the grain, aimed at people whose diet is mainly rice and lacks vitamin A.

core.h: Benefits of genetic engineering in medicine
core.p: Genetically modified microorganisms can make human proteins in large amounts. The best known example is **human insulin** made by GM bacteria for people with **type 1 diabetes**.
bullets: The human insulin gene is inserted into bacteria, which multiply in fermenters and make **human insulin**.
Produced in **large quantities**, quickly and relatively cheaply.
It is identical to human insulin, so fewer **allergic reactions** than insulin taken from pigs or cows.
No animals need to be killed, avoiding **ethical and religious** objections to animal insulin.
Other examples: human growth hormone, and some GM animals that produce human proteins in their milk.
In future, **gene therapy** may treat inherited disorders by inserting working alleles.

callouts.p: For insulin from GM bacteria, mention quantity, speed or cost, human form so fewer reactions, and no animals used.

core.p: Because GM is relatively new, some effects are uncertain. Many concerns are about what happens once GM organisms are released into the environment.
bullets: Genes could **transfer to wild relatives**, for example herbicide-resistance genes producing **superweeds**.
Bt toxins might harm **non-target insects** such as butterflies or bees, reducing **biodiversity**.
Insect pests may evolve **resistance** to the Bt toxin by natural selection.
Possible unknown **long-term health effects** of eating GM food, or **allergic reactions** to new proteins.
Growing large areas of the same GM variety (**monoculture**) reduces biodiversity and variation.
Fewer insect pests may mean less food for birds and other animals in the food chain.

callouts.p: Many health risks are possible or perceived rather than proven. Write may or could, not will.

core.p: Even when a technique works, there are practical issues about cost, time and control.
bullets: Genetic engineering needs **expensive** laboratories, equipment and skilled scientists.
GM seeds are often **patented** by large companies, so farmers may have to **buy new seed every year**, which poorer farmers may not afford.
GM products must pass long **safety testing** and regulation before use; some countries restrict or ban GM crops.
Selective breeding is cheap but **slow**, taking many years to produce a new variety.
Consumers may refuse to buy GM food, so it may need **labelling**.

core.p: **Ethics** is about whether something is right or wrong, not whether it works. Ethical arguments are opinions, so give **both sides**.
bullets: Some people believe it is wrong to **interfere with nature** or play God by moving genes between species.
**Animal welfare**: selectively bred or GM animals may suffer health problems.
Concerns that the same techniques could be used to change humans, for example to choose characteristics (designer babies).
**Who benefits?** Profits may go to big companies rather than poor farmers.
Some people have **religious** or personal objections, for example to genes from certain animals.
On the other side: it may be unethical **not** to use technology that can prevent blindness (golden rice), feed people or treat diabetes.

callouts.p: A question about whether something is morally right or wrong, which science alone cannot answer.

core.h: Golden rice as a case study
core.p: Golden rice shows the balance of benefits and concerns well and is a favourite exam context.
bullets: **Benefit**: could reduce vitamin A deficiency, which causes blindness and weakens the immune system, especially in children.
**Benefit**: rice is a staple food, so the vitamin source reaches people who need it.
**Concern**: genes may spread to other rice varieties.
**Concern**: may reduce the drive to provide a varied diet; some people distrust GM food.
**Concern**: cost and control of seed; it has been made available to poor farmers to address this.

core.p: Use a table like this to organise a balanced evaluation.
bullets: Both methods **increase food production** and improve characteristics.
Both can **reduce genetic variation** if only a few varieties are grown.
Genetic engineering raises extra concerns because genes cross **species barriers**.
Medicine examples (insulin) are usually seen as **more acceptable** than GM food because the benefit is clear and the GM bacteria are contained in fermenters.

head: Benefits
Risks
rows: Higher yield, disease resistance, more milk or meat, cheap
Inbreeding, genetic disorders, less variation, welfare problems
Pest and herbicide resistance, golden rice, less spraying
Gene transfer to wild plants, harm to insects, unknown long-term effects, seed cost
Large amounts of human insulin, fewer allergic reactions, no animals killed
Expensive to set up; ethical worries about modifying organisms

core.h: How to answer an evaluate question
core.p: In a 6-mark **evaluate** question you need benefits, risks and a **conclusion** that is justified by your points.
bullets: Start with benefits, using a named example (Bt crops, golden rice, insulin).
Then give risks, again specific (gene transfer, reduced variation, inbreeding).
Add a practical or ethical point.
Use any data in the question, for example yield figures or pesticide use.
Finish with a judgement: for example the benefits outweigh the risks if crops are tested and monitored.

callouts.p: Balanced, linked points plus a clear conclusion. A list of one-sided points cannot score full marks.

analogy.p: Selective breeding is like a family cooking only its favourite recipes for generations: dishes get better at what you like, but other recipes are forgotten and lost (reduced variation), and if one ingredient becomes unavailable you have no alternatives (disease risk). Genetic engineering is like cutting a single recipe out of a completely different cookbook and pasting it into yours: quick and precise, but the new recipe might be copied into neighbours' books without permission (gene transfer) and people argue about whether you should mix cookbooks at all (ethics). Where it breaks down: a recipe does not reproduce or spread itself, whereas living organisms do, and alleles are not deliberately chosen to be forgotten; variation is lost because only some parents breed.

terms.d: Choosing organisms with desired characteristics to breed together over many generations.
Changing an organism's genome by inserting a gene, often from another species, to give a desired characteristic.
An organism whose genome has been altered by genetic engineering.
Differences in alleles between individuals in a population.
All the alleles present in a population.
Breeding closely related individuals, increasing the chance of offspring inheriting two harmful recessive alleles.
A GM crop containing a gene from Bacillus thuringiensis so it produces a toxin that kills insect pests.
A GM crop that is not harmed by a weedkiller, so the weedkiller can be sprayed to kill weeds only.
GM rice that produces beta-carotene, which the body converts to vitamin A.
Insulin made by bacteria into which the human insulin gene has been inserted.
A weed that has gained a resistance gene (for example herbicide resistance) from a GM crop.
The variety of different species and genetic variation in an area.
Growing a single variety of crop over a large area.
Ideas about whether actions are morally right or wrong.
Legal ownership of an invention, such as a GM seed, so others must pay to use it.
Inserting working alleles into a person's cells to treat an inherited disorder.

mistakes.w: Selective breeding puts new genes into an organism.
mistakes.r: Selective breeding only combines alleles already present in the species; genetic engineering can add genes from another species.

mistakes.w: Selective breeding causes mutations.
mistakes.r: It reduces genetic variation; it does not cause mutations.

mistakes.w: Inbreeding creates diseases.
mistakes.r: Inbreeding increases the chance of inheriting two copies of a harmful recessive allele, causing genetic disorders.

mistakes.w: GM food is poisonous to humans.
mistakes.r: There may be unknown long-term effects or allergies; this is a possible risk, not a proven fact.

mistakes.w: Golden rice contains vitamin A.
mistakes.r: Golden rice produces beta-carotene, which the body converts into vitamin A.

mistakes.w: Insulin from bacteria is better because it is natural.
mistakes.r: It is identical to human insulin so causes fewer allergic reactions, can be made in large amounts, and no animals are needed.

mistakes.w: An ethical issue is that GM crops might not work.
mistakes.r: That is a practical issue. Ethical issues are about right and wrong, such as interfering with nature or animal welfare.

mistakes.w: Reduced variation means animals look the same.
mistakes.r: Reduced variation means fewer different alleles, so the population is less able to survive a new disease or environmental change.

exam.q: State one difference between selective breeding and genetic engineering.
model: Genetic engineering can use genes from a different species whereas selective breeding uses only the same species / genetic engineering is faster (one generation).
exam.tip: Make a direct comparison using whereas.

exam.q: Give two benefits of selective breeding in farm animals.
model: Any two: more milk; more meat; docile/gentle temperament; disease resistance; faster growth.
exam.tip: Give specific characteristics.

exam.q: Explain why selectively bred crops may be more at risk from a new disease.
model: Selective breeding reduces genetic variation / the gene pool.
So there may be no plants with alleles for resistance, so all the crop could be killed.
exam.tip: Link reduced variation to the lack of resistant individuals.

exam.q: Explain why inbreeding in dogs can lead to health problems.
model: Related dogs share many of the same alleles.
Increases the chance of offspring inheriting two copies of a harmful recessive allele, causing a genetic disorder.
exam.tip: Use the word recessive allele.

exam.q: Give two advantages of producing insulin using genetically modified bacteria rather than extracting it from pigs.
model: Large amounts can be produced quickly / cheaply.
It is human insulin so fewer allergic reactions / rejection.
No animals are killed / avoids ethical or religious objections (any two).
exam.tip: Two different ideas for two marks.

exam.q: Golden rice has been genetically modified. Explain how golden rice could improve human health.
model: It produces beta-carotene which is converted to vitamin A in the body.
This reduces vitamin A deficiency, which can cause blindness, in people whose diet is mainly rice.
exam.tip: Name the deficiency effect.

exam.q: Suggest one risk to the environment of growing herbicide-resistant crops.
model: The herbicide-resistance gene could transfer to wild plants / weeds by pollen.
Producing superweeds that cannot be killed by the herbicide.
exam.tip: Describe the route and the consequence.

exam.q: Give one ethical objection to genetic engineering.
model: Any one: interfering with nature / playing God; animal welfare; religious objection; could lead to modifying humans; unfair profits for large companies.
exam.tip: Make sure it is about right and wrong, not about whether it works.

exam.q: Some farmers in poorer countries cannot afford GM seed. Explain why this is a practical problem with GM crops.
model: GM seed is patented / expensive and must often be bought every year.
So the benefits of higher yields may not reach the farmers who need them most.
exam.tip: Link cost to who benefits.

exam.q: Evaluate the use of genetic engineering to produce insect-resistant crops.
model: Crops produce Bt toxin so insect pests are killed and fewer crops are lost.
Higher yields help feed a growing population.
Less insecticide spraying, saving money and reducing harm to other organisms.
But non-target insects such as butterflies could be harmed, reducing biodiversity.
Insects could evolve resistance to the toxin; genes could spread to wild plants.
Unknown long-term effects on health; seed may be costly; some people object ethically.
Conclusion: benefits outweigh risks if crops are carefully tested and monitored (or a justified opposite view).
exam.tip: Balanced points with a justified conclusion.

exam.q: Discuss the benefits and risks of selective breeding in agriculture.
model: Benefit: higher crop yields / more milk or meat.
Benefit: disease resistance in crops or animals; docile animals easier to handle.
Benefit: low cost and no special technology.
Risk: reduced genetic variation so whole populations vulnerable to new disease or environmental change.
Risk: inbreeding leads to genetic disorders from harmful recessive alleles.
Risk: health and welfare problems, for example breathing problems in some dog breeds or leg problems in broiler chickens.
exam.tip: Discuss means both sides; a conclusion is helpful but not always required.

worked.q: A GM insect-resistant cotton crop was introduced. Insecticide use fell from 12 kg per hectare to 3 kg per hectare. Calculate the percentage decrease and state one benefit of this.
steps: Decrease = 12 - 3 = 9 kg per hectare.
Percentage decrease = (9 / 12) x 100 = 75%.
Benefit: fewer non-target insects such as bees are killed, less pollution, and lower cost for the farmer.
worked.ans: 75% decrease; less harm to other species and lower cost.

worked.q: A wheat variety was selectively bred for yield. Yield rose from 2.4 to 6.0 tonnes per hectare over 50 years. How many times greater is the new yield, and what risk should the farmer consider?
steps: The yield is 2.5 times greater.
Risk: breeding from a few high-yielding plants reduces genetic variation, so a new disease could destroy the whole crop as no plants have resistance alleles.
worked.ans: 2.5 times greater; reduced genetic variation increases vulnerability to disease.

worked.q: Model answer: Suggest why many people accept GM bacteria producing insulin but are less willing to accept GM food crops.
steps: Insulin has a clear, direct medical benefit to people with diabetes.
GM bacteria are kept contained in fermenters, so genes cannot spread into the environment.
GM crops are grown in open fields, where genes might spread to wild plants and affect insects.
People eat GM crops directly and worry about unknown long-term health effects, whereas insulin is purified.
worked.ans: Insulin gives a clear benefit and is produced in contained conditions, while GM crops are released into the environment and eaten, raising environmental and health concerns.

bio_edx.3.2.summary: Antibiotic-resistant bacteria are strong modern evidence for Darwin's theory of evolution by natural selection, because we can watch it happen. A random **mutation** gives a bacterium **resistance**; when an antibiotic is used, non-resistant bacteria are killed but the resistant ones **survive and reproduce**, passing on the resistance allele. Because bacteria reproduce so quickly, a **resistant population** (such as **MRSA**) can develop within a short time, which is a serious problem for medicine.

core.p: **Antibiotics** are drugs that kill bacteria or stop them growing, for example penicillin. They treat **bacterial infections** only.
bullets: Antibiotics do **not** work against viruses, because viruses are not cells and live inside host cells.
Each antibiotic targets a structure or process in bacterial cells (e.g. building the cell wall).
Antibiotics damage bacterial cells but not human cells, so they can be taken safely.

callouts.p: When bacteria are no longer killed by an antibiotic, because they carry an allele that allows them to survive it.

core.h: Why bacteria are good evidence for evolution
core.p: Evolution in animals usually takes thousands of years, so it cannot be watched. Bacteria reproduce by **binary fission** as often as every **20 minutes**, so many generations pass in days and natural selection can be observed directly.
bullets: Huge population sizes mean even rare mutations appear regularly.
Each new generation inherits the alleles of its parent cell.
Scientists have observed populations becoming resistant after antibiotics came into widespread use: a change in inherited characteristics, which is **evolution**.

fig.cap: Bacteria can produce dozens of generations in a day, compared with one human generation in about 25 years, so evolution in bacteria is fast enough to observe.

core.p: Bacteria in a population vary. Occasionally a **random mutation** in a bacterium's DNA produces a **new allele** that makes it resistant to an antibiotic.
bullets: The mutation happens **by chance**, before the antibiotic is used.
The antibiotic does **not cause** the mutation.
At first only one or very few bacteria are resistant.

callouts.p: Bacteria are resistant, not immune. Immunity involves the immune system of animals.

core.h: Step 2: Antibiotic acts as a selection pressure
core.p: When a person takes an antibiotic, it **kills the non-resistant bacteria**. The resistant bacteria survive. The antibiotic is the **selection pressure**.
bullets: Resistant bacteria now have **less competition** for nutrients and space.
This gives them an even greater advantage.

core.p: The surviving resistant bacteria **reproduce** (binary fission) and **pass on the resistance allele** to their offspring.
bullets: All offspring of a resistant bacterium are genetically identical clones, so all are resistant.
The **population of resistant bacteria increases**.
The antibiotic no longer works, and the infection is hard to treat.

callouts.p: Mutation -> resistant allele -> antibiotic kills non-resistant -> resistant survive and reproduce -> pass on allele -> resistant population grows.

Antibiotic resistance

core.p: **MRSA** (meticillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus) is a bacterium resistant to several antibiotics. It is a well-known example of antibiotic resistance and spreads mainly in hospitals.
bullets: Strains resistant to many antibiotics are called **multiple-resistant** or 'superbugs'.
Infections are very hard to treat and can be fatal.
Hospitals contain many ill patients and much antibiotic use, so strong selection for resistance.

callouts.p: Meticillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus: the standard named example of an antibiotic-resistant bacterium.

core.p: The more antibiotics are used, the greater the selection pressure, so resistant strains are favoured more often.
bullets: **Overuse / over-prescription**, including for minor infections.
Prescribing for **viral** infections such as colds, where they have no effect but still select for resistance in other bacteria.
Patients **not finishing the course**, so some bacteria (the more resistant ones) survive.
Routine use in **farming** to keep animals healthy or promote growth.

core.p: Doctors, patients and farmers can all slow the development of resistant strains.
bullets: Only prescribe antibiotics when really needed, and **not for viral infections**.
Patients should **complete the full course** so all bacteria are killed.
Use specific antibiotics that target the particular bacterium.
**Reduce use in agriculture**.
Good **hygiene** in hospitals (hand washing, isolating infected patients) to stop resistant bacteria spreading.
Develop **new antibiotics**, although this is slow and expensive and resistance may evolve to them too.
