core.p: Antibiotic resistance shows evolution is happening now and has real consequences.
bullets: Some infections are becoming untreatable.
Routine operations become riskier if infections cannot be controlled.
It supports Darwin's theory with direct observation rather than fossils alone.

analogy.p: Spray a weed killer on a lawn full of weeds. If by chance a few weeds are naturally unaffected, they are the only ones left; with no competitors they spread and soon the whole lawn is full of weeds the spray cannot kill. The spray did not create the tough weeds, it just removed everything else. It breaks down because bacteria reproduce asexually in minutes and pass the allele to every offspring, and bacteria can even share resistance genes with each other.

terms.d: A drug that kills bacteria or stops their growth; it has no effect on viruses.
The ability of bacteria to survive treatment with an antibiotic, due to an allele they carry.
A random change in the base sequence of DNA that can produce a new allele.
A different version of a gene.
Individuals best adapted to their environment are more likely to survive, reproduce and pass on their alleles.
An environmental factor that affects survival; for bacteria, the antibiotic.
Asexual reproduction in bacteria in which one cell divides into two identical cells.
A genetically distinct type within a species of bacterium.
A strain of bacteria not killed by a particular antibiotic.
Meticillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus, a bacterium resistant to several antibiotics.
A change in the inherited characteristics of a population over time through natural selection.
A microorganism that causes disease.
Struggle between organisms for limited resources such as nutrients and space.

mistakes.w: The antibiotic causes the bacteria to mutate.
mistakes.r: Mutations are random and occur before the antibiotic is used; the antibiotic selects resistant bacteria.

mistakes.w: Bacteria become immune to antibiotics.
mistakes.r: Bacteria become **resistant**; immunity is a property of the host's immune system.

mistakes.w: The person becomes resistant to the antibiotic.
mistakes.r: The **bacteria** become resistant, not the patient.

mistakes.w: Antibiotics kill viruses.
mistakes.r: Antibiotics only work on bacteria; viruses are not affected.

mistakes.w: Resistant bacteria survive (and stop there).
mistakes.r: Resistant bacteria survive **and reproduce**, passing on the resistance allele.

mistakes.w: Bacteria get used to the antibiotic.
mistakes.r: A mutation gives some bacteria a resistance allele and natural selection increases their number.

mistakes.w: Finish the course so you don't get ill again.
mistakes.r: Finish the course so all bacteria are killed and no (partly resistant) bacteria survive to reproduce.

mistakes.w: Evolution in bacteria is fast because they mutate faster.
mistakes.r: It is fast mainly because bacteria **reproduce very quickly**, giving many generations in a short time.

exam.q: What does MRSA stand for?
model: Meticillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus.
exam.tip: Spell 'resistant' correctly.

exam.q: Name the process that first produces antibiotic resistance in a bacterium.
model: Mutation.
exam.tip: One word answer.

exam.q: Explain why antibiotics should not be prescribed for a cold.
model: Colds are caused by viruses.
Antibiotics do not kill viruses / it increases selection for resistant bacteria.
exam.tip: Two linked points.

exam.q: Explain why patients should complete the full course of antibiotics.
model: To make sure all the bacteria are killed.
So no bacteria survive to mutate / reproduce and form a resistant strain.
exam.tip: Link to resistance, not just getting better.

exam.q: Explain why the development of antibiotic resistance in bacteria is evidence for evolution.
model: It shows a change in the inherited characteristics of a population.
Due to natural selection, which can be observed because bacteria reproduce quickly.
exam.tip: Use the definition of evolution.

exam.q: Give two ways hospitals can reduce the spread of MRSA.
model: Hand washing / hand gel for staff and visitors.
Isolating infected patients / cleaning wards / limit antibiotic use.
exam.tip: Any two distinct measures.

exam.q: Explain how a population of bacteria can become resistant to an antibiotic.
model: Random mutation gives a bacterium an allele for resistance.
Antibiotic kills non-resistant bacteria.
Resistant bacteria survive and reproduce.
Pass on the resistance allele so resistant population increases.
exam.tip: This is the classic 4-marker; learn it in order.

exam.q: A graph shows that after an antibiotic was added the number of bacteria fell, then rose again. Explain the rise.
model: Some bacteria were resistant (due to mutation).
Resistant bacteria survived and had less competition.
They reproduced, so numbers increased.
exam.tip: Mention less competition for the third mark.

exam.q: Explain why the evolution of antibiotic resistance happens much faster than evolution in mammals.
model: Bacteria reproduce very quickly (e.g. every 20 minutes).
So many generations occur in a short time.
exam.tip: Generation time is the key idea.

exam.q: Discuss the causes of increasing antibiotic resistance and how it can be reduced.
model: Mutations give some bacteria resistance; antibiotic use selects for them.
Over-prescription / prescribing for viral infections increases selection pressure.
Not completing courses allows some bacteria to survive.
Use in farming increases resistance.
Reduce by prescribing only when needed and completing courses.
Hygiene and isolation in hospitals; developing new antibiotics.
exam.tip: Balance causes and solutions for the top level.

worked.q: A doctor gives a patient antibiotic A. After 5 days the patient is no better, and tests show the bacteria are resistant to A. Explain what has happened and suggest what the doctor should do.
steps: Some bacteria had a mutation making them resistant to A.
A killed the non-resistant bacteria; resistant bacteria survived.
Resistant bacteria reproduced and passed on the resistance allele.
Doctor should test which antibiotics still work and prescribe a different antibiotic.
worked.ans: Natural selection produced a population resistant to A; a different antibiotic that the bacteria are not resistant to should be used.

worked.q: A bacterium divides every 20 minutes. Starting from one resistant bacterium, how many resistant bacteria will there be after 4 hours (assuming none die)?
steps: Number of divisions in 4 hours = 240 / 20 = 12.
Each division doubles the number: 2^12.
worked.ans: 4096 resistant bacteria, showing how quickly a resistant population can grow.

worked.q: Data: in 2000, 5% of S. aureus samples in a hospital were MRSA; in 2010, 40% were. Describe and explain the trend.
steps: Describe: the percentage of MRSA increased from 5% to 40%, an eightfold increase over 10 years.
Explain: heavy antibiotic use in hospitals killed non-resistant bacteria.
Resistant bacteria survived, reproduced and spread between patients.
worked.ans: MRSA increased 8 times because antibiotic use selected resistant bacteria, which survived, reproduced and spread.

bio_edx.3.3.summary: Fossils and stone tools provide evidence that humans evolved from earlier hominid ancestors over millions of years. Key fossils are **Ardi** (4.4 million years old), **Lucy** (3.2 million years old) and **Turkana Boy**, found by **Richard Leakey's** team (1.6 million years old): over time, brain size increased, and skeletons show a change towards **walking fully upright**. Stone tools became **more complex** over time, and they can be dated from the **rock layers (strata)** they are found in, which suggests increasing brain size and intelligence.

core.p: Humans (**Homo sapiens**) belong to a group called **hominids**. Fossils show that we share a common ancestor with chimpanzees, and that several hominid species existed over the last few million years. We did **not** evolve from chimpanzees; we share an ancestor with them.
bullets: A **fossil** is the remains or traces of an organism preserved in rock.
Most early human fossils have been found in **East Africa** (Ethiopia, Kenya, Tanzania).
Fossils are compared for: **brain size (skull volume)**, leg and arm length, pelvis shape, foot structure and how the skull sits on the spine.
These features show how far a species could **walk upright (bipedalism)** and how intelligent it may have been.

callouts.p: The preserved remains or traces of an organism that lived long ago, usually found in rock.

core.p: **Ardi** (Ardipithecus ramidus) is a fossil skeleton found in **Ethiopia** in 1992 (by a team led by Tim White) and dated at **4.4 million years old**. It shows a mixture of ape-like and human-like features.
bullets: **Small brain**, about the size of a chimpanzee's (about 300 to 350 cm3).
Foot had an **ape-like big toe** pointing sideways (opposable) for **grasping branches and climbing**.
**Long arms** and short legs, like an ape.
Structure of the legs and pelvis suggests she could **walk upright** on two legs, although not as efficiently as humans.
Ardi lived in a woodland environment.

core.p: **Lucy** (Australopithecus afarensis) is a fossil skeleton found in **Ethiopia** in 1974 (by Donald Johanson), dated at **3.2 million years old**.
bullets: Brain **slightly larger** than Ardi's (about 400 to 450 cm3), but still similar to a chimpanzee's.
Feet had an **arch** and the **big toe was in line** with the other toes, more like a human's, so not adapted to grasping.
Leg bones and pelvis show she **walked upright** more efficiently than Ardi.
Arms and legs were in between ape and human proportions.
Fossilised footprints of the same species (found by **Mary Leakey** at Laetoli) also show upright walking.

core.h: Leakey's discovery: Turkana Boy (1.6 million years ago)
core.p: In **1984** a team led by **Richard Leakey** found an almost complete skeleton in **Kenya**, near Lake Turkana, called **Turkana Boy** (Homo erectus), dated at **1.6 million years old**.
bullets: **Much larger brain** (about 850 to 900 cm3), closer to human size.
**Short arms and long legs**, much more like a modern human than an ape.
Skeleton shows he was **fully adapted to walking upright**.
Homo erectus used more complex stone tools such as hand axes.
The Leakey family (Louis, Mary, Richard, Meave) found many important hominid fossils in East Africa.

callouts.p: Ardi 4.4 million years; Lucy 3.2 million years; Leakey's Turkana Boy 1.6 million years.

bullets: Over time: brain volume **increases**, arms get **shorter** relative to legs, the foot changes from **grasping** to **walking**.
These trends support the idea that humans evolved gradually from ape-like ancestors.

callouts.p: Brain sizes are estimates; exam papers give their own values, so always use the numbers in the question.

core.h: Why brain size and walking upright matter
core.p: Two big trends in human evolution are **increasing brain size** and **bipedalism**. Scientists link these to survival advantages.
bullets: Walking upright frees the hands for carrying food and **using tools**.
Upright walking is energy-efficient over long distances on open grassland and allows seeing over tall grass.
A larger brain allows more complex behaviour: **making tools, communicating, cooperating and planning**.
These advantages would have been selected by **natural selection** over many generations.

core.p: As well as bones, early humans left **stone tools**. Tools are useful evidence because stone does not decay, so many more tools survive than bones.
bullets: Tools become **more complex and specialised** over time.
More complex tools need more **planning and skill**, suggesting **larger brains** and increasing intelligence.
Tool design links to how species lived: hunting, butchering, scraping skins, making clothes.

core.h: Development of stone tools over time
core.p: Learn the sequence of species and tools. Each species made more sophisticated tools than the one before.
bullets: Simple pebble tools were made by striking one stone against another to make a sharp edge.
Later tools were shaped on both sides and later still made from flakes struck from a prepared core.

core.h: Dating tools from their environment: stratigraphy
core.p: Tools can be dated from where they are found. Rock forms in **layers (strata)**, with newer layers laid down on top of older ones. This is called **stratigraphy**.
bullets: **Deeper layers are older**; layers near the surface are younger.
A tool found in a deep layer is older than one in a layer above it.
This gives a **relative** age (older or younger than) unless a layer can be dated.

callouts.p: The study of rock layers (strata); older layers are found below younger layers.

fig.cap: Rock strata: the deeper the layer, the older the tools in it. A dated volcanic ash layer gives an actual age for the layers above and below it.

core.p: Scientists combine methods to get accurate ages for fossils and tools.
bullets: **Radiometric dating** of **volcanic rock / ash** layers above or below a tool gives a real age range, e.g. a tool between ash dated 2.0 and 1.8 million years must be between those ages.
**Carbon-14 dating** can be used on **organic material** found with tools (bones, wood, charcoal from fires), but only for remains up to about 50 000 years old.
Comparing tool **style** with tools of known age from other sites.

callouts.p: If asked how tools are dated 'from their environment', describe stratigraphy (deeper = older) and dating of nearby volcanic ash or organic material.

core.p: Fossil and tool evidence is incomplete, so conclusions can change as new finds are made.
bullets: Fossils form only in rare conditions, so the **fossil record is incomplete**.
Many fossils are **partial** skeletons, so features must be estimated.
Rock layers can be disturbed (earthquakes, erosion), mixing old and new.
Different species existed at the **same time**, so human evolution is a branching tree, not a straight line.

analogy.t: A family photo album with missing pages
analogy.p: The fossils are like a few surviving photos from a very old family album: each photo (Ardi, Lucy, Turkana Boy) shows the family at a different time, and placing them in date order shows gradual changes such as bigger heads and longer legs. The stone tools are like the gadgets on the shelf in each photo, becoming more advanced in later pictures. It breaks down because the 'family' is a branching tree of different species, not a single line of parents and children, and most of the pages have been lost.

terms.d: A member of the group of primates that includes humans and their extinct close relatives (and great apes).
The preserved remains or traces of an organism that lived long ago.
Ardipithecus ramidus fossil from Ethiopia, about 4.4 million years old; small brain, grasping big toe, could walk upright.
Australopithecus afarensis fossil from Ethiopia, about 3.2 million years old; walked upright, brain slightly larger than Ardi's.
Homo erectus skeleton found by Richard Leakey's team in Kenya in 1984, about 1.6 million years old; larger brain, short arms, long legs.
Walking upright on two legs.
A big toe that points away from the other toes so it can grip, used for climbing.
The size of the brain, estimated from the volume of the skull, in cm3.
Tools made from shaped stone by early humans; they became more complex over time.
The study of rock layers; deeper layers are older than layers above them.
Layers of sedimentary rock.
Using the decay of radioactive isotopes in rock, such as volcanic ash, to find its age.
Dating organic material using the decay of carbon-14; works for remains up to about 50 000 years old.
Modern humans, appearing about 200 000 years ago.

mistakes.w: Humans evolved from chimpanzees.
mistakes.r: Humans and chimpanzees share a **common ancestor**.

mistakes.w: Lucy is older than Ardi.
mistakes.r: Ardi is older (4.4 million years); Lucy is 3.2 million years.

mistakes.w: Rock layers at the top are oldest.
mistakes.r: **Deeper** layers are older; layers near the surface are younger.

mistakes.w: Carbon dating is used to date stone tools.
mistakes.r: Stone contains no carbon from living things; carbon dating is used on organic material found with the tools, and volcanic ash is dated radiometrically.

mistakes.w: Ardi could not walk upright.
mistakes.r: Ardi could walk upright but also had an opposable big toe for climbing.

mistakes.w: Tools got bigger over time.
mistakes.r: Tools became **more complex / refined / specialised** over time.

mistakes.w: More complex tools show humans got stronger.
mistakes.r: More complex tools suggest **larger brains / greater intelligence**.

mistakes.w: Turkana Boy was found by Louis Leakey in Ethiopia.
mistakes.r: Turkana Boy was found by **Richard Leakey**'s team in **Kenya** in 1984.

exam.q: Give the approximate age of the fossil Ardi.
model: 4.4 million years.
exam.tip: Include 'million'.

exam.q: State how the size of the brain changed from Ardi to Turkana Boy.
model: It increased.
exam.tip: Use data if given.

exam.q: Describe one feature of Ardi's foot and what it suggests about how Ardi moved.
model: Opposable / sideways big toe.
For grasping branches / climbing trees.
exam.tip: Feature plus function.

exam.q: Give two features of Lucy's skeleton that show she walked upright.
model: Arched foot / big toe in line with other toes.
Pelvis / leg bones similar to humans.
exam.tip: Two separate structural features.

exam.q: Explain why stone tools found deeper in the ground are older than tools found higher up.
model: Rock / sediment layers are laid down over time.
So newer layers are on top of older layers.
exam.tip: Name stratigraphy if you can.

exam.q: Describe how the age of a stone tool could be estimated.
model: Stratigraphy: depth of rock layer; deeper is older.
Radiometric dating of volcanic ash layers above / below the tool.
Carbon dating of organic remains (bones, charcoal) found with the tool.
exam.tip: Three different methods for three marks.

exam.q: Describe how stone tools changed from Homo habilis to Homo sapiens.
model: Homo habilis: simple pebble tools made by hitting rocks together.
Homo erectus: larger, shaped hand axes.
Neanderthals: more complex flint tools / spear points.
Homo sapiens: finer tools such as arrowheads and needles.
exam.tip: Name the species in order.

exam.q: Explain how the evidence from stone tools supports the idea that brain size increased during human evolution.
model: Tools became more complex over time.
Making complex tools needs greater intelligence / planning, linked to a larger brain.
exam.tip: Link tool complexity to brain.

exam.q: Compare the fossils of Ardi, Lucy and Turkana Boy as evidence for human evolution.
model: Ardi 4.4 mya, Lucy 3.2 mya, Turkana Boy 1.6 mya show a sequence over time.
Brain size increased: about 350, 450 and 900 cm3.
Ardi had an opposable big toe for climbing; Lucy and Turkana Boy had human-like feet.
Ardi walked upright but also climbed; Lucy walked upright; Turkana Boy fully upright.
Arms became shorter and legs longer, more human-like.
Gradual change in features supports evolution from a common ancestor.
exam.tip: Use comparative words: larger, shorter, more upright.

exam.q: Suggest why the fossil evidence for human evolution is incomplete.
model: Fossils only form in rare conditions / most remains decay.
Many fossils not yet found / destroyed by geological activity.
exam.tip: Two different reasons.

worked.q: A tool is found between two volcanic ash layers. The ash below is dated at 1.9 million years and the ash above at 1.7 million years. What is the age of the tool and which species probably made it?
steps: Layers below are older, layers above are younger.
So the tool is younger than 1.9 million years and older than 1.7 million years.
Homo erectus lived from about 2.0 million years ago and made hand axes; Homo habilis also overlaps this range.
Check the tool's style: a symmetrical hand axe suggests Homo erectus; a simple pebble tool suggests Homo habilis.
worked.ans: Between 1.7 and 1.9 million years old; probably Homo erectus (hand axe) or Homo habilis (pebble tool) depending on its complexity.

worked.q: Ardi's brain was about 350 cm3 and Turkana Boy's about 900 cm3. Calculate the percentage increase.
steps: Increase = 900 - 350 = 550 cm3.
Percentage increase = 550 / 350 x 100.
worked.ans: About 157% increase in brain volume over 2.8 million years.

worked.q: Explain how Lucy's skeleton shows she was more adapted to walking upright than Ardi.
steps: Compare the feet: Ardi had an opposable big toe for climbing; Lucy's big toe was in line with the other toes and her foot was arched.
Compare legs and pelvis: Lucy's were more human-like.
Conclude: Lucy's features are better suited to walking on two legs, and less suited to climbing.
worked.ans: Lucy had an arched foot, a big toe in line with the other toes and a more human-like pelvis and legs, so she walked upright more efficiently than Ardi.

bio_edx.3.4.summary: The **pentadactyl limb** is a limb with **five digits** built on the same basic bone plan: one upper bone (humerus), two lower bones (radius and ulna), wrist bones (carpals), palm bones (metacarpals) and finger bones (phalanges). It is found in mammals, birds, reptiles and amphibians, even though their limbs do very different jobs such as grasping, flying, swimming and running. The best explanation for the same bone plan being used for different functions is that all these animals **evolved from a common ancestor** that had a pentadactyl limb, and **natural selection** then modified the limb to suit each environment. This makes the pentadactyl limb important **evidence for evolution**.

core.p: Penta means five and dactyl means finger, so a pentadactyl limb is a limb that ends in **five digits**. The important point is not just the number five but that the **same arrangement of bones** appears in the arms, legs, wings and flippers of many different vertebrates.
bullets: Found in **vertebrates** with four limbs: **mammals, birds, reptiles and amphibians**
Same bone plan in the **forelimb** of a human, bat, whale, bird, horse and mole
The bones may be **lengthened, shortened, fused or lost**, but the overall pattern can still be recognised
Fish fins do not have this plan, so fish are not used as pentadactyl examples

callouts.p: A limb with five digits, made of the same basic arrangement of bones, found in many different vertebrates.

core.p: Every pentadactyl limb is built from the same sections in the same order, starting nearest the body. Learning this order lets you spot the pattern in any limb an exam shows you.
bullets: **One bone** in the upper limb: the **humerus**
**Two bones** in the lower limb: the **radius** and the **ulna**
A group of **wrist bones**: the **carpals**
**Palm bones**: the **metacarpals** (five, one leading to each digit)
**Digit bones**: the **phalanges**, forming **five digits**
Pattern to remember: **1 bone, 2 bones, many small bones, 5 digits**

callouts.t: Use the pattern, not just the names
callouts.p: Edexcel questions usually reward saying the limbs have the same bones in the same arrangement. Naming humerus, radius and ulna adds detail and precision.

core.p: The striking observation is that the limbs look very different on the outside and do very different jobs, yet the bones inside follow the same plan.
bullets: **Human arm**: long digits and a movable thumb for **grasping** and manipulating objects
**Bat wing**: very **long metacarpals and phalanges** stretch a skin membrane for **flying**
**Whale or dolphin flipper**: **short, flattened** humerus, radius and ulna with **extra phalanges** inside a paddle for **swimming**
**Bird wing**: digits **reduced and fused**, long humerus, radius and ulna to support feathers for **flying**
**Horse leg**: mainly **one long digit** (the others reduced) ending in a hoof for **fast running**
**Mole forelimb**: short, broad bones and strong digits for **digging**

head: Animal
Function
How the plan is modified
rows: Five long, separate digits; opposable thumb
Very long metacarpals and phalanges support a wing membrane
Short, flat bones; many phalanges in a flipper
Digits reduced and fused; strong long arm bones
One main digit, others reduced; hoof

core.p: Limbs that share the same underlying structure because they were inherited from a common ancestor are called **homologous structures**. They may now have different functions.
bullets: Homologous means **same origin**, not necessarily the same job
The pentadactyl limb is the classic example of a homologous structure
Homologous structures suggest the animals are **related**
The more similar the structure, the more **closely related** the organisms are likely to be

callouts.p: Structures in different species that have the same basic structure because they were inherited from a common ancestor, even if they now have different functions.

core.h: Why it is evidence for evolution
core.p: Scientists ask: why would a bat, a whale and a human all use one bone, then two bones, then wrist bones, then five digits, when their limbs do completely different jobs? The best explanation is shared ancestry.
bullets: All these vertebrates share the **same basic bone structure**
This suggests they all **evolved from a common ancestor** that had a pentadactyl limb
Over millions of years each group lived in **different environments**
**Natural selection** favoured different limb shapes in each environment
So the limb was **modified (adapted)** for different functions, but the **underlying plan was kept**
If each species had appeared separately, there would be no reason for them to share the same bone plan

callouts.p: Same bone structure in different species, used for different functions, shows they share a common ancestor and have evolved by natural selection.

core.h: How natural selection modified the limb
core.p: The pentadactyl limb links directly to Darwin's theory. The ancestral limb was not designed for flying or swimming; it was gradually changed generation by generation.
bullets: There was **variation** in limb bones within the ancestral population, caused partly by **mutations**
In a given environment, some variations were **advantageous** (e.g. slightly longer digits for gliding)
Individuals with these variations were **more likely to survive and reproduce**
They **passed on the alleles** for the advantageous limb shape to their offspring
Over **many generations** the advantageous form became more common
Different populations in different environments were modified in different directions: this is **divergent evolution**

callouts.t: Do not say animals change their limbs on purpose
callouts.p: Individuals do not adapt during their lifetime because they need to. Variation already exists and natural selection acts on it over many generations.

core.p: The pentadactyl limb shows that groups we think of as very different (mammals, birds, reptiles, amphibians) are related.
bullets: The common ancestor was an early **four-limbed vertebrate (tetrapod)**
Mammals, birds, reptiles and amphibians **all descended** from it
The limb pattern helps scientists build **evolutionary trees** showing relationships
Species whose limbs differ less from each other usually shared a **more recent** common ancestor

core.p: Not every similar-looking structure is evidence of a close common ancestor. It helps to compare the inside structure, not just the job.
bullets: **Homologous**: same structure, can have different functions (bat wing and human arm)
**Analogous**: same function, different structure (bat wing and insect wing)
An insect wing has **no bones** at all, so it is not a pentadactyl limb
Bat and bird wings are both pentadactyl limbs, but they evolved flight **separately** and their bones are arranged differently along the wing

callouts.p: Analogous structures are not named in the Edexcel spec, but knowing the contrast helps you explain why the pentadactyl limb counts as evidence.

core.h: Strengths and limits of this evidence
core.p: Grade 9 answers evaluate evidence. The pentadactyl limb strongly supports evolution, but it is one line of evidence among several.
bullets: **Strength**: found across a very wide range of vertebrates, so the pattern is not a coincidence
**Strength**: matches what natural selection predicts: old structures modified, not new ones invented
**Limit**: it shows species are related, but not exactly **when** they diverged
**Limit**: it is **indirect** evidence; it supports the theory rather than proving it
It agrees with other evidence: **fossils**, **antibiotic-resistant bacteria** and **DNA comparisons**

callouts.p: Say the pentadactyl limb provides evidence for or supports evolution. Avoid saying it proves evolution.

core.p: Different lines of evidence point the same way, which makes the theory of evolution much stronger.
bullets: **Fossils** of early tetrapods show limbs with digits, matching the predicted common ancestor
Fossils of early whales show **back legs** and pentadactyl front limbs that became flippers over time
**DNA comparisons** show the same groups are related, in the same pattern suggested by limb structure
When independent evidence agrees, scientists have more confidence in the conclusion

core.p: Exams often show a diagram of a limb you have not seen, such as a frog, crocodile or penguin, and ask you to use it as evidence.
bullets: Step 1: **identify** the humerus (one bone), radius and ulna (two bones), carpals and digits
Step 2: **compare** with a human arm: same bones, same order
Step 3: **state the function** of the new limb and how bones are changed (longer, shorter, fused, lost)
Step 4: **conclude**: shared plan, so common ancestor; differences due to natural selection for different environments

callouts.p: Quote what you can see: for example, the bones of the digits are much longer in the bat. Marks are given for linking the diagram to the explanation.

core.p: For a full-mark answer on the pentadactyl limb, make sure you can do every item here.
bullets: Describe the structure: **five digits**, 1 bone then 2 bones then wrist then digits
Name at least three animals and their **different functions**
State that the limbs have the **same basic structure**
Explain this means they share a **common ancestor**
Explain that **natural selection** modified the limb for different environments
Use the term **homologous** where it fits
Say this is **evidence for** evolution (not proof)

analogy.p: Think of the pentadactyl limb as a family recipe for a basic dough: flour, water, yeast, salt. Over generations, different branches of the family changed it into pizza, bread rolls, naan and pretzels to suit local tastes. The final dishes look and taste different, but the shared base recipe shows they came from the same original kitchen, just as the shared bone plan shows animals came from a common ancestor. Where it breaks down: cooks change recipes on purpose to suit a plan, but evolution has no plan or goal. Limbs change only because random variations that happen to help survival are passed on more often, over many generations.

terms.d: A limb with five digits and the same basic arrangement of bones, found in mammals, birds, reptiles and amphibians.
A finger or toe.
The single bone of the upper forelimb.
The two bones of the lower forelimb (forearm).
The small bones of the wrist.
The bones of the palm, one leading to each digit.
The bones that make up the digits.
Structures with the same basic structure in different species, inherited from a common ancestor, which may have different functions.
Structures with the same function but a different basic structure, which did not come from a shared ancestral structure.
An ancestral species from which two or more different species have evolved.
A change in the inherited characteristics of a population over time through natural selection, which may result in new species.
The process by which individuals with advantageous variations are more likely to survive and reproduce, passing on their alleles.
A feature that makes an organism well suited to its environment and function.
When populations from a common ancestor evolve in different directions because they live in different environments.
An animal with a backbone.
A four-limbed vertebrate; the group that includes amphibians, reptiles, birds and mammals.

mistakes.w: The limbs are the same, so the animals are the same species.
mistakes.r: The limbs have the same basic bone structure, which shows the species share a common ancestor; they are still different species.

mistakes.w: The animals all look similar.
mistakes.r: The limbs look very different and have different functions, but the bones inside have the same arrangement.

mistakes.w: Whales grew flippers because they needed to swim.
mistakes.r: Variation already existed; individuals with flipper-like limbs survived and reproduced more, passing on alleles over many generations.

mistakes.w: The pentadactyl limb proves evolution.
mistakes.r: It provides evidence that supports the theory of evolution.

mistakes.w: Pentadactyl means having four limbs.
mistakes.r: Pentadactyl means having five digits.

mistakes.w: Humans evolved from bats (or whales).
mistakes.r: Humans, bats and whales evolved from a shared common ancestor; none evolved from the other living species.

mistakes.w: Insect wings are pentadactyl limbs because they are used for flying like bat wings.
mistakes.r: Insect wings have no bones; similar function does not mean the same structure. The pentadactyl limb is about shared bone structure.

mistakes.w: They have the same bones so they have the same function.
mistakes.r: They have the same structure but different functions; the bones are modified (different lengths, fused or lost) for each function.

mistakes.w: The limb shows the animals are similar.
mistakes.r: State the conclusion precisely: the animals are related and evolved from a common ancestor.

exam.q: What does the term pentadactyl mean?
model: Having five digits (fingers or toes)
exam.tip: One word answers like five are often not enough: say five digits.

exam.q: Name the single bone found in the upper part of every pentadactyl forelimb.
model: Humerus
exam.tip: Spelling must be close enough to be recognisable.

exam.q: Give two groups of vertebrates that have a pentadactyl limb.
model: Any two from: mammals, birds, reptiles, amphibians
exam.tip: Fish is wrong: fins are not pentadactyl limbs.

exam.q: A human arm and a bat wing look very different. Describe one similarity in their structure.
model: Both have one upper bone, two lower bones, wrist bones and five digits (the same arrangement of bones)
exam.tip: Name a specific shared feature, such as both having a radius and ulna.

exam.q: Describe how the forelimb of a whale is different from a human arm, and explain how this suits its function.
model: Whale has shorter, flatter bones / more phalanges, enclosed in a flipper
Forms a paddle that pushes against water for swimming / steering
exam.tip: One mark for the difference, one for linking it to function.

exam.q: Explain how the pentadactyl limb provides evidence for evolution.
model: Different species have the same basic bone structure in their limbs
Suggests they evolved from a common ancestor
exam.tip: The common ancestor point is the key mark.

exam.q: Explain why the limbs of bats, whales and humans have the same arrangement of bones but different shapes.
model: They share / evolved from a common ancestor with a pentadactyl limb
The species lived in different environments
Natural selection favoured different variations in each environment
So the limb was modified / adapted for different functions (flying, swimming, grasping) while keeping the same basic structure
exam.tip: Include both the shared plan (ancestry) and the differences (natural selection).

exam.q: State the name given to structures that have the same basic structure but different functions in different species.
model: Homologous structures
exam.tip: Do not confuse with analogous.

exam.q: A student says that a butterfly wing and a bird wing show that butterflies and birds share a recent common ancestor. Evaluate this statement.
model: The statement is incorrect / not supported
Butterfly wing has no bones / different structure from the pentadactyl bird wing, so similar function does not show shared ancestry
exam.tip: Evaluate means give a judgement and a reason.

exam.q: Explain how natural selection could have led to the long digits in a bat wing from an ancestor with shorter digits.
model: Variation in digit length in the ancestral population (due to mutation)
Individuals with longer digits could glide or fly better, so caught more food / escaped predators
These individuals were more likely to survive and reproduce
Passed on alleles for longer digits; over many generations the long-digit wing became common
exam.tip: Use the sequence: variation, advantage, survive, reproduce, pass on alleles, many generations.

exam.q: Discuss how the anatomy of the pentadactyl limb supports Darwin's theory of evolution by natural selection. Refer to at least three animals in your answer.
model: Pentadactyl limb has one upper bone (humerus), two lower bones (radius, ulna), carpals, metacarpals and phalanges with five digits
Same arrangement found in many vertebrates, e.g. human, bat, whale (bird, horse)
Limbs have different functions: grasping (human), flying (bat), swimming (whale)
Bones are modified: long digits in bat, short flat bones in whale flipper, separate digits in human
Same structure suggests all evolved from a common ancestor
Different environments meant natural selection favoured different variations
Advantageous variations passed on over many generations, so limbs adapted while keeping the same plan
Supported by other evidence such as fossils and DNA; is evidence, not proof
exam.tip: Six-markers are marked on levels: describe the structure, give examples, then build a linked explanation using common ancestor and natural selection.

worked.q: A diagram shows the forelimb of a mole. It has a short, wide humerus, a short radius and ulna, carpals and five broad digits. Use the diagram to explain how the mole forelimb provides evidence for evolution.
steps: Identify the bones: one upper bone (humerus), two lower bones (radius and ulna), wrist bones and five digits
Compare: this is the same arrangement of bones as in a human arm, so it is a pentadactyl limb
Function: the mole uses its forelimb for digging; the short, wide, strong bones give a powerful shovel
Explain: the same structure in species with different functions suggests a common ancestor
Explain the difference: natural selection in an underground environment favoured short, strong limbs
worked.ans: The mole limb has the same bone plan as a human arm (humerus, radius and ulna, carpals, five digits) but is short and broad for digging. This shared structure suggests moles and humans evolved from a common ancestor, and natural selection modified the limb for burrowing.

worked.q: Model answer: Explain why scientists think birds and mammals are related, using the pentadactyl limb.
steps: State the observation: bird wings and mammal forelimbs both contain a humerus, radius, ulna, carpals and digits
Note the differences: in birds the digits are reduced and fused, in mammals they are usually separate
Link to ancestry: the shared arrangement is best explained by both groups inheriting it from a common ancestor
Link to natural selection: in birds, variations that supported feathers and flight were selected over many generations
worked.ans: Birds and mammals share the same pentadactyl bone plan in their forelimbs, so they are thought to have evolved from a common tetrapod ancestor; natural selection modified the bird limb (fused, reduced digits) for flight.

worked.q: Applied example: A newly discovered fossil reptile has a forelimb with one upper bone, two lower bones, wrist bones and five digits, all very short and flattened. What can scientists suggest about it?
steps: The bone plan is pentadactyl, so the reptile is a tetrapod related to other vertebrates with this limb
Short, flattened bones are similar to a whale or turtle flipper
Suggest it lived in water and used the limb for swimming
This is an example of the same basic structure being adapted to a different function by natural selection
worked.ans: It shares a common ancestor with other tetrapods, and its flattened pentadactyl limb suggests it was adapted for swimming.

bio_edx.3.5.summary: **Classification** is sorting living organisms into groups based on their similarities. For a long time organisms were placed into **five kingdoms** (animals, plants, fungi, protists and prokaryotes) using features you can see, such as cell structure and how they get their food. In the 1970s **Carl Woese** used **genetic analysis** (comparing the base sequences of RNA and DNA) and found that the prokaryotes were really two very different groups. This led to the **three-domain system**: **Archaea**, **Bacteria** and **Eukarya**, which better reflects how organisms are related through evolution.

core.h: What classification is and why we do it
core.p: There are millions of species, so scientists group them to make them easier to study, name and compare. Modern classification also tries to show **evolutionary relationships**: which organisms share a more recent common ancestor.
bullets: Classification = putting organisms into **groups** based on **similarities and differences**
Helps scientists **identify** and **name** organisms consistently around the world
Shows how organisms are **related** and how they **evolved**
Useful for **conservation**: knowing which species are most distinct or endangered
Classification systems **change** as new evidence (such as DNA data) is found

callouts.p: Organising living organisms into groups based on their shared characteristics.

core.p: Organisms are placed into a series of groups, from very large to very small. Each group contains organisms with more features in common than the group above it.
bullets: Order of groups (largest to smallest): **domain, kingdom, phylum, class, order, family, genus, species**
Memory aid: **D**ear **K**ing **P**hilip **C**ame **O**ver **F**or **G**ood **S**oup
Moving down the hierarchy, groups contain **fewer organisms** that are **more similar**
The **species** is the smallest group: organisms that can **interbreed to produce fertile offspring**
Each species has a two-part **binomial name**: **genus** then **species**, e.g. **Homo sapiens**

callouts.p: The three-domain system added a new top level above kingdom. Kingdoms still exist inside the domains.

core.p: The five-kingdom system (proposed by Robert Whittaker in 1969) sorted organisms using **observable characteristics**, mainly seen with a microscope: whether cells have a nucleus, whether they have cell walls, whether they are unicellular or multicellular and how they feed.
bullets: **Animals**: multicellular, **no cell wall**, no chloroplasts, feed on other organisms (heterotrophic)
**Plants**: multicellular, **cellulose cell wall**, **chloroplasts**, make food by **photosynthesis**
**Fungi**: mostly multicellular with **hyphae** (yeast is unicellular), **chitin** cell wall, no chloroplasts, feed by **extracellular digestion** (saprophytic)
**Protists (protoctists)**: mostly **unicellular** **eukaryotes**, e.g. Amoeba, Plasmodium, Chlorella
**Prokaryotes**: unicellular, **no nucleus**, circular DNA and plasmids, e.g. bacteria

callouts.t: Based on what you can see
callouts.p: The five kingdoms were decided using structural features and nutrition, not genetic information.

core.p: Classifying by appearance can be misleading. Organisms can look similar without being closely related, and the microscope cannot see differences in biochemistry and genes.
bullets: All prokaryotes were placed in **one kingdom** because they all **lack a nucleus** and look similar
The protist kingdom was a **mixed group** of organisms that did not fit elsewhere
Similar features can evolve **separately** in unrelated organisms, so appearance does not always show ancestry
The system did not use evidence about **genes**, which were not easy to sequence at the time

core.p: Advances in technology allowed scientists to read the **sequence of bases** in DNA and RNA. Comparing sequences between organisms shows how closely they are related.
bullets: Organisms that are **closely related** have **more similar** base sequences
The more **differences** there are, the longer ago the groups **shared a common ancestor**
Scientists compare a gene or molecule that **all organisms have**, so every organism can be compared fairly
Carl Woese compared the sequences of **ribosomal RNA (rRNA)**, which is found in the ribosomes of every cell
Genetic analysis can reveal relationships that are **not visible** from structure

callouts.p: Comparing the base sequences of DNA (or RNA) from different organisms to find how closely related they are.

core.h: Carl Woese and the three domains
core.p: In 1977 the American microbiologist **Carl Woese** compared rRNA sequences from many organisms. He found that some prokaryotes, then called archaebacteria, were **as different from bacteria as bacteria are from humans**. In 1990 he proposed the **three-domain system**.
bullets: Prokaryotes split into **two separate domains**: **Archaea** and **Bacteria**
All organisms with a nucleus placed together in the domain **Eukarya**
Archaea have some genes and features **more similar to eukaryotes** than to bacteria
The three domains are thought to have **separated very early** in the history of life
Accepted because it is based on **molecular evidence** that reflects **evolutionary relationships**

callouts.p: Genetic analysis (comparing base sequences) showed that prokaryotes are two very different groups, so the five kingdoms were replaced by three domains: Archaea, Bacteria and Eukarya.

core.p: Each domain is a large group of organisms with a shared evolutionary origin. You should be able to describe what is in each.
bullets: **Archaea**: prokaryotes (no nucleus); often live in **extreme environments** such as hot springs, salt lakes and deep-sea vents; cell membranes and cell walls chemically **different** from bacteria
**Bacteria**: 'true' bacteria; prokaryotes; found almost everywhere; include many that cause disease and many that are useful, e.g. **E. coli**, **Lactobacillus**
**Eukarya**: organisms whose cells have a **nucleus** and membrane-bound organelles; includes the kingdoms **protists, fungi, plants and animals**

Nucleus
Examples

rows: Four of the five old kingdoms

callouts.t: Archaea are not a type of bacteria
callouts.p: Archaea and bacteria both lack a nucleus, but genetic analysis shows they are separate domains. Do not call archaea bacteria in a three-domain answer.

core.h: How the five kingdoms fit into the three domains
core.p: The new system did not throw away the old groups entirely. It added the domain level and split the prokaryote kingdom.
bullets: Kingdom **prokaryotes** is split into **two domains**: Archaea and Bacteria
Kingdoms **animals, plants, fungi and protists** all go into the domain **Eukarya**
So the biggest genetic divisions in life are among the **prokaryotes**, not between plants and animals
Plants and animals look very different but are **more closely related** to each other than archaea are to bacteria

core.p: This is a good example of how science works: new evidence led to a new model, which was checked and accepted by other scientists.
bullets: New **technology** (sequencing) made new evidence available
The evidence was **repeatable**: other scientists found the same patterns
Ideas were published and **peer reviewed**
The new system **explained** observations the old one could not, such as unusual archaeal biochemistry
It shows that scientific classification is **tentative**: it can change with new evidence

callouts.p: Questions may ask why the classification changed. The answer is new evidence from genetic analysis, made possible by new technology.

core.p: The three-domain system is linked to evolution. Groups are based on shared ancestry, so classification becomes a kind of family tree of life.
bullets: Base sequences change by **mutation** over time
Two species that separated **recently** have had less time to build up differences, so their sequences are **more similar**
This lets scientists draw **evolutionary trees** showing common ancestors
Genetic evidence agrees with other evidence such as **fossils** and **anatomy** (for example the pentadactyl limb)

core.p: Exams often ask you to compare the systems or explain the difference. Focus on the evidence each uses.
bullets: Five kingdoms: based on **observable features** (structure, nutrition)
Three domains: based on **genetic analysis** (base sequences, especially rRNA)
Five kingdoms: **one** prokaryote group; three domains: **two** prokaryote domains
Three domains adds a **new level above kingdom**
Three domains better reflects **evolutionary relationships**

core.p: Before the exam, make sure you can do all of the following for this point.
bullets: Name the **five kingdoms** and give a feature of each
Name the **three domains** and say which organisms are in each
State that the change came from **genetic analysis** (comparing DNA or RNA base sequences)
Explain that this showed **prokaryotes are two distinct groups**
Explain that closer relatives have **more similar** sequences
Name **Carl Woese**
Put the hierarchy in order from **domain to species**

analogy.t: Sorting a library by cover or by content
analogy.p: The five-kingdom system is like sorting library books by the colour and size of their covers: quick, and often useful, but two books with similar covers might be on totally different subjects. Genetic analysis is like actually reading the text inside and grouping books by how many sentences they share. Woese read the 'text' of rRNA and found that the shelf labelled prokaryotes actually held two very different sets of books, so a new top-level section was needed. Where it breaks down: books are written by authors who can copy from any other book, but organisms mainly inherit their sequences from ancestors, and sequence differences build up gradually by mutation over time.

terms.d: Organising living organisms into groups based on their shared characteristics.
The highest level of classification; there are three domains: Archaea, Bacteria and Eukarya.
The level of classification below domain, e.g. animals, plants, fungi.
A classification system that groups organisms into animals, plants, fungi, protists and prokaryotes based on observable features.
A classification system that groups organisms into Archaea, Bacteria and Eukarya based on genetic analysis.
Comparing the base sequences of DNA or RNA in different organisms to find out how closely they are related.
The order of bases (A, T, C, G in DNA; A, U, C, G in RNA) along a nucleic acid molecule.
The RNA found in ribosomes, present in all cells; Woese compared its sequence between organisms.
A single-celled organism with no nucleus; its DNA is free in the cytoplasm.
An organism whose cells contain a nucleus and membrane-bound organelles.
A domain of prokaryotes, often found in extreme environments, genetically distinct from bacteria.
A domain of prokaryotes containing the true bacteria.
The domain containing all eukaryotes: protists, fungi, plants and animals.
A mostly unicellular eukaryote that is not an animal, plant or fungus, e.g. Amoeba.
A group of organisms that can interbreed to produce fertile offspring.
The two-part scientific name of a species: genus followed by species, e.g. Homo sapiens.
The scientist who used rRNA sequence comparisons to propose the three-domain system.

mistakes.w: The three domains are animals, plants and bacteria.
mistakes.r: The three domains are Archaea, Bacteria and Eukarya.

mistakes.w: The system changed because scientists looked more closely with microscopes.
mistakes.r: It changed because of genetic analysis: comparing DNA / RNA base sequences.

mistakes.w: Archaea are a type of bacteria.
mistakes.r: Archaea are a separate domain; genetic analysis shows they are as different from bacteria as from eukaryotes.

mistakes.w: The five kingdoms were deleted.
mistakes.r: A domain level was added above kingdom; the prokaryote kingdom was split into Archaea and Bacteria and the other four kingdoms are in Eukarya.

mistakes.w: Organisms with very different DNA are closely related.
mistakes.r: Closely related organisms have more similar base sequences; more differences mean a more distant common ancestor.

mistakes.w: Fungi are plants because they do not move.
mistakes.r: Fungi are a separate kingdom: chitin cell walls, no chloroplasts, feed saprophytically.

mistakes.w: Eukarya contains organisms with no nucleus.
mistakes.r: Eukarya contains organisms whose cells have a nucleus; prokaryotes (no nucleus) are in Archaea and Bacteria.

mistakes.w: Hierarchy: kingdom, domain, phylum, order, class...
mistakes.r: Correct order: domain, kingdom, phylum, class, order, family, genus, species.

exam.q: Name the three domains in the three-domain system of classification.
model: Archaea, Bacteria and Eukarya (all three needed)
exam.tip: Spell Archaea and Eukarya carefully.

exam.q: Name the five kingdoms.
model: Animals, plants, fungi
Protists (protoctists), prokaryotes
exam.tip: Usually 2 marks for all five, 1 mark for three or four.

exam.q: State what type of evidence led scientists to propose the three-domain system.
model: Genetic analysis / comparing DNA or RNA base sequences
exam.tip: Name the evidence, not just 'new technology'.

exam.q: Which domain contains fungi?
model: Eukarya
exam.tip: All organisms with a nucleus are in Eukarya.

exam.q: Give two features used to place an organism in the fungi kingdom.
model: Cell wall made of chitin
No chloroplasts / do not photosynthesise / feed saprophytically / made of hyphae
exam.tip: Avoid just 'they are mushrooms'.

exam.q: Describe how genetic analysis has led to the three-domain system replacing the five-kingdom system.
model: Scientists (Woese) compared base sequences of DNA / rRNA from different organisms
Organisms with more similar sequences are more closely related
Found that prokaryotes formed two very different groups
So prokaryotes were split into Archaea and Bacteria, with all eukaryotes in Eukarya
exam.tip: This is the exact wording of the spec point: learn a four-step answer.

exam.q: Explain why comparing DNA sequences gives a more reliable classification than comparing appearance.
model: Organisms can look similar without being closely related / similar features can evolve separately
DNA differences build up over time, so similarity in sequences directly reflects how recently species shared a common ancestor
exam.tip: Link sequence similarity to common ancestry.

exam.q: Archaea and bacteria are both prokaryotes. Explain why they are placed in different domains.
model: Genetic analysis shows their base sequences (rRNA) are very different
So they are not closely related / they separated very early in evolution
exam.tip: Lacking a nucleus is the similarity; genes are the difference.

exam.q: Give the correct order of the classification groups, starting with the largest.
model: Domain, kingdom, phylum, class
Order, family, genus, species
exam.tip: Use a memory aid such as Dear King Philip Came Over For Good Soup.

exam.q: Suggest why the three-domain system was accepted by other scientists.
model: The evidence (sequence data) was repeated / reproduced by other scientists / peer reviewed
It better explains evolutionary relationships than the five-kingdom system
exam.tip: Think about how science checks new ideas.

exam.q: Evaluate the five-kingdom system and the three-domain system as ways of classifying organisms.
model: Five kingdoms based on observable features such as cell structure and nutrition
Advantage: features are easy to observe without specialist equipment
Disadvantage: appearance can be misleading; organisms may look alike but not be related
All prokaryotes in one kingdom, and protists a mixed group
Three domains based on genetic analysis of base sequences (rRNA)
Showed prokaryotes are two distinct groups, Archaea and Bacteria; eukaryotes in Eukarya
Better reflects evolutionary relationships / common ancestry
Judgement: three-domain system is more accurate, though it needs sequencing technology and may still change with new evidence
exam.tip: Evaluate means weigh up both sides and give a reasoned judgement at the end.

worked.q: The table shows the percentage of the base sequence of one gene that is the same in four organisms compared with species A: species B 96%, species C 71%, species D 88%. Which species is most closely related to A, and which shared a common ancestor with A longest ago?
steps: Higher percentage similarity means fewer differences in the base sequence
Fewer differences means less time for mutations to build up, so a more recent common ancestor
Species B has the highest similarity (96%), so it is most closely related to A
Species C has the lowest similarity (71%), so it shared a common ancestor with A longest ago
Order of relatedness to A: B (96%) then D (88%) then C (71%)
worked.ans: B is most closely related to A; C shared a common ancestor with A longest ago.

worked.q: An organism found in a hot spring is single-celled and has no nucleus. Its rRNA base sequence is very different from E. coli. Which domain should it be placed in? Explain your answer.
steps: No nucleus means it is a prokaryote, so it is not in Eukarya
Prokaryotes are in Archaea or Bacteria
Its rRNA sequence is very different from E. coli, which is a bacterium
Living in an extreme environment (hot spring) is typical of many archaea
Genetic evidence, not appearance, decides the domain
worked.ans: Archaea: it is a prokaryote, but its rRNA sequence is very different from bacteria, and it lives in an extreme environment.

worked.q: Model answer (4 marks): Describe how genetic analysis led to the three-domain system.
steps: Point 1: Carl Woese compared the base sequences of ribosomal RNA from many organisms
Point 2: The more similar the sequence, the more closely related the organisms
Point 3: He found that prokaryotes (once one kingdom) were two very different groups
Point 4: So a new top level, the domain, was created: Archaea, Bacteria and Eukarya
worked.ans: Comparing rRNA / DNA base sequences showed that prokaryotes are two genetically distinct groups, so they were split into Archaea and Bacteria, with all eukaryotes in Eukarya, replacing the five kingdoms with three domains.

bio_edx.3.6.summary: **Selective breeding** (also called **artificial selection**) is when **humans choose** plants or animals with **desired characteristics** and breed them together, repeating this over **many generations** so the characteristic becomes more common. It has transformed food plants (such as high-yield, disease-resistant wheat and the many vegetables bred from wild cabbage) and domesticated animals (such as high-milk-yield dairy cows and fast-growing chickens). It has greatly increased **food production**, but it also **reduces genetic variation**, which can make populations vulnerable to disease and can cause **inbreeding** and **health and welfare problems**.

core.p: Humans have been selectively breeding plants and animals for thousands of years, ever since farming began. The idea is simple: breed from the best individuals, and the next generation is more likely to have the features you want.
bullets: Humans **choose** the parents, not the environment
Breeding is for characteristics **useful to humans**, not necessarily to the organism
Works because many characteristics are **inherited** (controlled by genes and their alleles)
Has to be repeated for **many generations** to have a big effect
Also called **artificial selection**, the term Darwin used to compare it with natural selection

callouts.p: When humans choose organisms with desired characteristics and breed them together, over many generations, so the offspring show those characteristics.

core.p: Exam questions often ask you to describe how a farmer or breeder would produce a new variety. Learn the steps in order.
bullets: 1. Decide which **characteristic** is wanted (e.g. high milk yield)
2. Choose **parents** that show the characteristic most strongly from a **varied population**
3. **Breed** them together (cross-pollinate plants or mate animals)
4. From the **offspring**, select those with the characteristic most strongly
5. **Breed these** together
6. **Repeat over many generations** until all offspring reliably show the characteristic

callouts.p: The mark scheme almost always gives a mark for 'repeat over many generations'. Selecting once is not enough.

core.h: Why it works: genes and alleles
core.p: Selective breeding changes how common particular alleles are in a population.
bullets: Individuals vary partly because they have **different alleles**
The chosen parents carry the alleles for the **desired characteristic**
Offspring **inherit** these alleles, so more of them show the characteristic
Unwanted alleles are not passed on because individuals carrying them are **not bred from**
Over time the desired alleles become **more frequent** and other alleles may be **lost** from the population

callouts.p: Selective breeding increases the frequency of the alleles for the desired characteristic in the population.

core.p: Most crops we eat today look very different from their wild ancestors because of selective breeding.
bullets: **Higher yield**: more grain, fruit or seeds per plant
**Disease resistance**: e.g. wheat resistant to fungal diseases such as rust
**Pest resistance**, **drought tolerance** or cold tolerance to grow in more places
**Shorter stems** in wheat so plants put more energy into grain and do not fall over in wind
**Better taste**, bigger or sweeter fruit, longer shelf life
Crops that **ripen at the same time**, making harvesting easier

core.p: Edexcel expects you to describe the impact on food plants. Examples you can use:
bullets: **Wheat**: bred from wild grasses into high-yield, short-stemmed, disease-resistant varieties that feed billions of people

**Wild cabbage (Brassica oleracea)**: selected for different parts to give **cabbage** (leaves), **broccoli** and **cauliflower** (flower heads), **Brussels sprouts** (side buds) and **kale** (leaves)
**Maize (corn)**: bred from a wild grass (teosinte) with tiny cobs into plants with large cobs of many kernels
**Bananas**: cultivated bananas are bred to be seedless with soft flesh

head: Crop
Wild ancestor
Characteristic selected
rows: High yield, short stem, disease resistance

core.p: Farm animals and pets have been selectively bred for features useful to humans.
bullets: **Dairy cattle** (e.g. Holstein-Friesian): very **high milk yield**
**Beef cattle**: more **muscle (meat)** and fast growth
**Chickens**: broilers that grow **very fast** for meat; laying hens that produce **many eggs**
**Sheep**: more and finer **wool**
**Pigs**: leaner meat and large litters
**Dogs**: gentle temperament, herding or guarding behaviour
Many animals are also bred for **docile (calm) behaviour**, making them easier to handle

core.p: Selective breeding has been hugely important for feeding the world's growing population.
bullets: **Increased food yields** from the same amount of land
**Disease-resistant crops** need fewer pesticides and fail less often
Crops can grow in **difficult conditions** (drought, cold, salty soil), improving **food security**
More **efficient** animals: more milk, meat or eggs per animal
Produces animals that are **easier and safer** to farm
Does **not need advanced technology**; any farmer can do it

core.p: The biggest scientific problem is the loss of variety in the gene pool.
bullets: Only a few individuals are bred from, so many **alleles are lost**
The population becomes **genetically very similar**
If a **new disease** appears, there may be **no individuals with resistance alleles**, so the whole crop or herd could be affected
Less variation means the population **cannot adapt** as well to **environmental change**
Lost alleles may have been **useful in the future** (e.g. for a new climate)

callouts.p: A selectively bred population has fewer alleles, so a new disease or change in conditions could wipe out many individuals.

core.p: Breeding closely related animals together (inbreeding) is often needed to fix a characteristic, but it causes problems.
bullets: **Inbreeding** increases the chance of offspring inheriting **two copies of a harmful recessive allele**
This raises the risk of **genetic disorders** (e.g. hip problems in some dog breeds, breathing difficulty in flat-faced dogs)
Animals bred for one feature may suffer **health problems**: fast-growing broiler chickens can have **leg problems** and heart problems
High-yield dairy cows can be more prone to **lameness** and **mastitis**
Raises **ethical concerns** about animal welfare
Can take **a long time** (many generations) and results are **not always predictable**

callouts.p: Selective breeding does not insert genes from another species. It only uses alleles already present in the species, mixed by normal reproduction.

core.p: Both change allele frequencies over many generations, but the selecting agent is different.
bullets: **Natural selection**: the **environment** selects; individuals best suited to survive reproduce more
**Selective breeding**: **humans** select; individuals with characteristics useful to humans are bred
Natural selection tends to keep features that help **survival**; selective breeding may produce features that **harm** survival in the wild (e.g. very heavy chickens)
Both depend on **variation** and **inheritance** of alleles

core.p: These are often compared in 6-mark questions on the benefits and risks of each (spec point 4.14). Here is the key difference to keep in mind.
bullets: Selective breeding uses **existing variation** within a species
Genetic engineering **transfers a gene** from one organism to another, often from a **different species**
Selective breeding is **slower** (many generations) and less precise; many alleles are carried along together
Genetic engineering can produce a change in **one generation** and is more targeted

core.p: Make sure you can do all of these for this point.
bullets: Define selective breeding / artificial selection
Describe the **steps**, including **repeat over many generations**
Give examples of **plant** characteristics and crops (wheat, wild cabbage varieties)
Give examples of **animal** characteristics (milk yield, meat, eggs, wool, temperament)
Explain **benefits** for food production
Explain **reduced genetic variation** and why this makes organisms vulnerable to **disease**
Explain **inbreeding** and **genetic disorders / welfare** problems

analogy.t: A playlist built by skipping songs
analogy.p: Imagine a music app that only plays more of the songs you choose to replay and drops the ones you skip. After months, your playlist is full of exactly the kind of songs you like: that is selective breeding increasing the desired alleles. But the playlist has lost huge variety, and if your taste suddenly changes, there is nothing different left to choose from, just as a selectively bred crop may have no resistance alleles left when a new disease arrives. Where it breaks down: you can search for and add brand new songs at any time, but a breeder can only work with alleles already present in the population (new ones only appear slowly by mutation, or by crossing with wild varieties).

mistakes.w: Breed the best two and you get the result.
mistakes.r: Select and breed the best offspring again, repeating over many generations.

mistakes.w: Selective breeding increases genetic variation.
mistakes.r: It reduces genetic variation because only a few individuals are bred and many alleles are lost.

mistakes.w: Selective breeding puts genes from another species into the organism.
mistakes.r: That is genetic engineering; selective breeding only uses alleles already in the species.

mistakes.w: Inbreeding causes mutations.
mistakes.r: Inbreeding increases the chance of inheriting two copies of an existing harmful recessive allele, causing genetic disorders.

mistakes.w: The crops become immune to all diseases.
mistakes.r: They may be resistant to particular diseases, but low variation makes the population vulnerable to new diseases.

mistakes.w: The animals choose the best partners.
mistakes.r: Humans choose which individuals breed; that is what makes it artificial selection.

mistakes.w: Selective breeding is the same as natural selection.
mistakes.r: In selective breeding humans select for characteristics useful to them; in natural selection the environment selects for survival.

mistakes.w: Offspring learn the characteristic from their parents.
mistakes.r: The characteristic is inherited through alleles passed on in gametes.

exam.q: What is meant by selective breeding?
model: Humans choosing organisms with desired characteristics to breed together (over many generations)
exam.tip: Include the idea that humans do the choosing.

exam.q: Give two characteristics that farmers might selectively breed for in crop plants.
model: Any two from: high yield, disease resistance, pest resistance, drought tolerance, short stems, better taste, larger fruit
exam.tip: Be specific: 'better' on its own does not score.

exam.q: Give one characteristic that might be selectively bred for in dairy cattle.
model: High milk yield (or docile temperament / disease resistance)
exam.tip: Match the characteristic to the animal's use.

exam.q: Describe how a farmer could use selective breeding to produce a herd of cows with a high milk yield.
model: Select a cow and bull with high milk yield (bull from high-yield mothers)
Breed them together
Select offspring with the highest milk yield and breed them
Repeat over many generations
exam.tip: A bull cannot produce milk: mention choosing a bull whose mother or daughters had a high yield for extra precision.

exam.q: Explain why selective breeding reduces genetic variation.
model: Only a small number of individuals with the desired characteristic are bred from
So alleles carried by other individuals are not passed on / are lost from the population
exam.tip: Talk about alleles being lost.

exam.q: Explain why a population of selectively bred crop plants could be badly affected by a new disease.
model: Low genetic variation / plants are genetically similar
So few or no plants carry alleles for resistance; most/all could be killed
exam.tip: Link low variation to lack of resistant individuals.

exam.q: Explain how inbreeding in selectively bred dogs can lead to health problems.
model: Closely related dogs share many of the same alleles
Increased chance of offspring inheriting two copies of a harmful recessive allele
Leads to genetic disorders, e.g. hip or breathing problems
exam.tip: Use the word recessive.

exam.q: Broccoli, cabbage and Brussels sprouts were all bred from wild cabbage. Explain how such different vegetables came from one species.
model: Wild cabbage population showed variation
Different breeders selected for different characteristics (flower buds, leaves, side buds)
Repeated selective breeding over many generations produced different varieties
exam.tip: Point out that different features were selected in different lines.

exam.q: State one difference between selective breeding and natural selection.
model: In selective breeding humans choose which individuals reproduce; in natural selection the environment does
exam.tip: Give both sides of the comparison.

exam.q: Suggest why selective breeding of fast-growing chickens raises ethical concerns.
model: Chickens grow so fast that they can develop leg / heart problems
Causes pain or suffering / poor animal welfare
exam.tip: Ethics questions need a reason linked to welfare or fairness.

exam.q: Discuss the impact of selective breeding on food plants and domesticated animals.
model: Process: humans select parents with desired characteristics, breed, select best offspring, repeat over many generations
Plants: higher yield, disease resistance, e.g. wheat; varieties of wild cabbage; helps food security
Animals: higher milk yield in dairy cows, more meat, more eggs, docile behaviour
Benefit: more food from the same land; more efficient farming
Drawback: reduced genetic variation, so vulnerable to new diseases or environmental change
Drawback: inbreeding increases harmful recessive alleles leading to genetic disorders
Drawback: welfare problems, e.g. broiler chickens leg problems, cows prone to mastitis
Balanced conclusion: has greatly increased food production but needs careful management of variation and welfare
exam.tip: Level 3 answers cover plants AND animals, benefits AND drawbacks, with linked explanations.

worked.q: Model answer (4 marks): A plant breeder wants a wheat variety resistant to a fungal disease. Describe how she could produce it by selective breeding.
steps: Grow a large, varied population of wheat and expose it to the fungus
Select the plants that show the most resistance (least infected)
Cross-pollinate these resistant plants and collect their seeds
Grow the offspring, expose to the fungus again, and select the most resistant
Repeat over many generations until all plants are reliably resistant
worked.ans: Select resistant parents, cross them, select the most resistant offspring, and repeat for many generations until all plants are resistant.

worked.q: A farmer measures average milk yield in her herd: generation 1 = 6000 litres per cow per year, generation 4 = 7200 litres. Calculate the percentage increase, and suggest one risk of continuing this breeding.
steps: Increase = 7200 - 6000 = 1200 litres
Percentage increase = (increase / original) x 100
Risk: continuing to breed only from the highest-yield cows reduces genetic variation, so the herd could be vulnerable to a new disease; high-yield cows may also suffer more mastitis or lameness
worked.ans: 20% increase; risk of reduced genetic variation (disease vulnerability) and welfare problems.

worked.q: Applied example: Explain why seed banks store seeds of wild and old varieties of crop plants.
steps: Selective breeding has reduced genetic variation in modern crops
Wild and old varieties contain alleles that modern varieties have lost
These alleles might give resistance to new diseases or tolerance of new climates
Breeders can cross modern crops with stored varieties to bring these alleles back
worked.ans: To preserve alleles lost through selective breeding, so they can be used in future to breed crops able to cope with new diseases or environmental change.

bio_edx.3.7.summary: **Tissue culture** is growing cells or tissues in a sterile, controlled environment outside the organism, on or in a **growth medium** containing nutrients (and, for plants, **plant hormones**). Because the new cells come from **mitosis**, every plant or cell produced is a **genetically identical clone** of the original. This lets plant breeders make large numbers of plants with **desirable characteristics** quickly and lets medical researchers test drugs and study disease on identical cells instead of whole animals.

core.p: Tissue culture means taking a small group of cells (or a small piece of tissue) from an organism and growing it in a container in the lab under **aseptic (sterile)** conditions. The cells are given everything they need: water, nutrients, the right temperature and, for plants, the right balance of hormones. The cells divide by **mitosis**, so all the cells produced are **genetically identical** to the original cells.
bullets: Used for **plants** (to produce whole new plants, often called micropropagation) and for **animal or human cells** (to grow layers of cells for research).
It is a form of **asexual reproduction / cloning**: no gametes and no fertilisation are involved.
Only **mitosis** happens, so there is no new genetic variation.
It must be done in **sterile conditions** because microorganisms (bacteria and fungi) grow very well on the same nutrient medium and would out-compete or kill the cells.
This is a **triple (separate science) only** point on the Edexcel spec: Paper 1, Topic 4.

callouts.p: Growing cells or tissues in a growth medium containing nutrients, in sterile conditions, outside the organism, to produce genetically identical cells or organisms.
All the new cells are made by mitosis from the original cells, so they all have exactly the same DNA (alleles) as the parent.

core.h: Why plants can be cloned from tiny pieces
core.p: Many plant cells, especially those in **meristems** (the growing regions at shoot tips and root tips), keep the ability to divide and to **differentiate** into any type of plant cell throughout the plant's life. Most animal cells lose this ability early on. This is why a tiny piece of a plant can grow into a whole new plant, but a piece of skin cannot grow into a whole animal.
bullets: Meristem cells are plant **stem cells**: unspecialised and able to divide repeatedly by mitosis.
With the right hormones, these cells can become root, stem, leaf or flower cells.
The tissue sample taken is called an **explant**.
Shoot tips are often chosen because meristem tissue is usually **free of viruses**, giving disease-free plants.

callouts.p: In a 6-mark answer, link tissue culture to mitosis and to plant stem cells in meristems. Examiners reward the idea that the cells are unspecialised and can differentiate.

core.h: The process of plant tissue culture, step by step
core.p: You need to be able to describe the method in order. Learn the six steps and the reason behind each one.
bullets: **1. Select** a parent plant with the **desired characteristics** (for example high yield, attractive flowers or disease resistance).
**2. Cut** small pieces of tissue (**explants**), usually from the **shoot tip** or another region with meristem cells, using a sterile scalpel.
**3. Sterilise** the explants (for example with dilute bleach or alcohol) and rinse with sterile water, to kill microorganisms on the surface.
**4. Place** the explants on a sterile **agar growth medium** containing **nutrients** (glucose, mineral ions such as nitrates, vitamins) and **plant hormones** (auxins and cytokinins).
**5.** The cells **divide by mitosis** to form a **callus**, a lump of **undifferentiated** cells. The callus can be divided to make many more cultures.

**6.** The callus is moved to media with **different hormone ratios** to stimulate **shoots and roots** to grow (differentiation). The plantlets are then transferred to **compost** in a greenhouse to grow into mature plants.

callouts.p: The cells divide by mitosis. Meiosis makes gametes and would produce variation, which is the opposite of what tissue culture does.
