core.h: What is in the growth medium and why
core.p: Each ingredient in the medium has a job. Exam questions often ask why a certain substance is added.
bullets: **Agar jelly**: a solid support that holds the tissue in place and contains water.
**Glucose (sugar)**: a source of energy for respiration, because the explant cannot yet photosynthesise enough.
**Mineral ions such as nitrates**: needed to make **amino acids and proteins** for growth; magnesium is needed for chlorophyll.
**Vitamins**: help normal cell function.
**Plant hormones (auxins and cytokinins)**: control cell division and which tissues form.
Kept at a **suitable temperature** and with light so plantlets can start to photosynthesise.

callouts.p: Changing the ratio of plant hormones in the medium decides whether the callus forms roots or shoots. Higher auxin tends to favour roots; higher cytokinin tends to favour shoots.

core.p: The growth medium is rich in sugar and nutrients, which makes it an ideal food for bacteria and fungi. If microorganisms get in, they grow much faster than the plant cells, use up the nutrients and may produce toxins, so the culture dies.
bullets: Sterilise tools (scalpels, forceps) by flaming or autoclaving.
Sterilise the surface of the explant with dilute bleach or ethanol, then rinse with sterile water.
Use sterile, sealed containers and work in a clean area (for example a laminar flow cabinet).
Contamination is one of the main **disadvantages**: one contaminated culture can be lost entirely.

callouts.p: For 2 marks, say what is done (sterilise / aseptic technique) AND why (to prevent microorganisms growing and competing with or killing the plant cells).

core.p: Plant breeders use tissue culture to make lots of copies of a plant that has the exact characteristics they want. Because the plants are clones, every one has the **same desirable features**.
bullets: **Large numbers** of plants can be produced **quickly** from one parent plant (thousands from a few cells).

Every plant is **genetically identical**, so desirable characteristics (for example high yield or a particular flower colour) are **reliably kept**. With seeds, characteristics can be lost because sexual reproduction mixes alleles.
Plants can be grown **all year round**, regardless of season, and need **little space**.
Can produce **disease-free** plants by using virus-free meristem tissue.
Can quickly bulk up a **new variety** made by selective breeding or genetic modification.
Useful for plants that are **hard to grow from seed** or produce few seeds (for example some orchids, bananas).
Can be used to **conserve rare or endangered plant species** by producing many individuals from a few cells.

callouts.p: Tissue culture = many identical plants, quickly, with the desired characteristics, in a small space, at any time of year.

core.p: Animal and human cells can also be grown in tissue culture. Cells are kept in flasks of liquid **culture medium** containing nutrients, at body temperature (37 °C). They grow as identical layers of cells that scientists can study and test.
bullets: Scientists can **test new drugs** on cultured cells or tissues to see if they are **toxic** or effective before testing on whole animals or people.
This **reduces the number of animals** used in testing.

Because all the cells are **genetically identical**, any difference in results is due to the drug (the **independent variable**), not genetic differences, so results are **more valid and reliable** (repeatable).
Allows study of how **diseases** such as cancer develop, and how cells grow and respond to chemicals, in a controlled way.
Large numbers of identical cells can be grown for many repeats and for comparison with **controls**.
Cells or tissues can be grown for **transplant research** (for example skin grafts for burns) and to study stem cells.

callouts.p: Cells in a flask do not behave exactly like a whole organism: there are no organ systems, no blood supply, no immune system. So drugs still have to go through animal and human clinical trials.

core.h: Disadvantages and risks of tissue culture
core.p: Because every plant is a clone, the biggest problem is the **lack of genetic variation**.
bullets: **No genetic variation**: if a new disease or pest attacks, **all** the plants are equally susceptible and the whole crop could be wiped out.
A lack of variation reduces the **gene pool**, so the population is less able to **adapt** to environmental change (fewer alleles for natural selection to act on).
**Expensive**: needs laboratories, sterile equipment and trained staff.
**Labour intensive** and needs careful technique.
**Contamination** with bacteria or fungi can destroy cultures.
Any **undesirable** characteristic or hidden fault in the parent is copied into every plant.

callouts.p: For an 'evaluate' or 'discuss' question, give advantages AND disadvantages, then a conclusion, for example: useful for producing uniform crops quickly, but farmers should keep other varieties to maintain genetic variation.

core.h: Tissue culture compared with other ways of producing plants
core.p: You may be asked to compare tissue culture with growing from seed or with taking cuttings.
bullets: **Seeds** come from sexual reproduction (meiosis, gametes and fertilisation), so offspring vary.
**Cuttings** are a simpler form of cloning: a piece of stem is cut and planted, often using rooting powder (auxin). It is cheap, but produces far fewer plants than tissue culture.
**Tissue culture** produces the most plants from the least material but is the most expensive.

core.h: Links to selective breeding and genetic modification
core.p: Tissue culture is often used together with the other techniques in Topic 4.
bullets: After **selective breeding** produces a plant with a useful combination of characteristics, tissue culture can make many identical copies quickly instead of waiting many generations.
In **genetic modification**, a gene may be inserted into a few plant cells; tissue culture is then used to grow these cells into whole GM plants.
Like selective breeding, tissue culture **reduces genetic variation** in crops.

callouts.p: Selective breeding and GM create the desirable plant; tissue culture copies it in large numbers.

core.p: Tissue culture of plants raises few ethical issues. Tissue culture of human and animal cells for research raises more questions, but is generally seen as reducing harm because it cuts the number of animals used.
bullets: Supports the aim of **replacing, reducing and refining** animal experiments.
Some human cell lines come from donated tissue, so **consent** is important.
Uniform crops make harvesting and selling easier (same size, ripen at the same time), which benefits farmers and supermarkets.

core.p: Edexcel questions on this point usually ask you to describe the process, explain why plants are identical, or give advantages in plant breeding or medical research.
bullets: Use key words: **explant, sterile, agar, nutrients, plant hormones, mitosis, callus, differentiate, genetically identical, clone**.
Always give a **reason** after an advantage: 'many plants quickly, **so** farmers can sell a new variety sooner'.
In medical research answers, mention **genetically identical cells**, **fewer animals** and **testing drugs for toxicity**.
For disadvantages, the key mark is **no genetic variation, so all susceptible to the same disease**.

callouts.p: 'Describe' = say what happens in order. 'Explain' = say what happens AND why. 'Evaluate' = pros, cons and a judgement.

analogy.p: Tissue culture is like putting one perfect page into a photocopier and printing thousands of identical copies. The sterile room keeps dust (microbes) off the copies, the paper and ink are the nutrients, and the copier settings are the hormones that decide what gets printed (roots or shoots). Seeds are more like asking two authors to write a new page together: every page comes out a bit different. Where it breaks down: a photocopy is made all at once from the original, but in tissue culture the cells copy themselves by mitosis and must then grow and differentiate into different tissues, which needs time, energy and the right hormone signals.

terms.d: Growing cells or tissues in a growth medium containing nutrients, under sterile conditions, to produce genetically identical cells or organisms.

A mass of undifferentiated plant cells formed when an explant divides by mitosis on a growth medium.
An organism or cell that is genetically identical to its parent.

A jelly made from seaweed used as a solid growth medium that supports tissue and holds water and nutrients.
The substance containing water, nutrients and sometimes hormones in which cells or tissues are grown.
Chemicals such as auxins and cytokinins that control plant growth; in tissue culture they control cell division and root or shoot formation.
Reproduction involving one parent and no gametes, producing genetically identical offspring.
Differences in alleles between individuals of the same species.
Producing large numbers of identical plants from small pieces of tissue using tissue culture.
Growing animal or human cells in a flask of nutrient medium, for example to test drugs.
How harmful a substance, such as a new drug, is to cells or organisms.

mistakes.r: The cells divide by mitosis, so all new cells are genetically identical.

mistakes.w: The plants are similar to the parent.
mistakes.r: The plants are genetically identical to the parent (clones).

mistakes.w: Sterile conditions are used to keep the plants clean.
mistakes.r: Sterile conditions prevent microorganisms growing on the nutrient medium and competing with or killing the plant cells.

mistakes.w: Tissue culture creates new varieties with new characteristics.
mistakes.r: Tissue culture copies an existing plant; it does not create new characteristics or variation.

mistakes.r: Glucose is added as an energy source for respiration.

mistakes.w: A disadvantage is that the plants are weak.
mistakes.r: A disadvantage is no genetic variation, so all plants are susceptible to the same disease or pest.

mistakes.w: Tissue culture in medicine means no animal testing is needed.
mistakes.r: It reduces the number of animals used, but drugs still need testing in whole organisms and clinical trials.

mistakes.w: Hormones are added to make the plant grow faster.
mistakes.r: Plant hormones (auxins and cytokinins) control cell division and stimulate the callus to form roots and shoots.

mistakes.w: The callus is made of specialised cells.
mistakes.r: The callus is a mass of undifferentiated cells that can later differentiate.

exam.q: State what is meant by a clone.
model: An organism that is genetically identical to its parent.
exam.tip: Use the phrase 'genetically identical', not 'the same' or 'similar'.

exam.q: Name the type of cell division that takes place in plant tissue culture.
model: Mitosis.
exam.tip: Spell it correctly; 'meiosis' scores zero.

exam.q: Give two substances that are added to the agar used in plant tissue culture.
model: Nutrients such as glucose / sugar.
Mineral ions such as nitrates / plant hormones such as auxins.
exam.tip: Be specific: 'food' is too vague.

exam.q: Explain why the tissue culture is carried out in sterile conditions.
model: To prevent contamination by microorganisms / bacteria / fungi.
Microorganisms would grow on the nutrients and compete with or kill the plant cells.
exam.tip: Give what (prevent microorganisms) and why (they compete/kill).

exam.q: Explain why plants produced by tissue culture all have the same characteristics as the parent plant.
model: Cells divide by mitosis.
So they are genetically identical to the parent / clones / have the same alleles.
exam.tip: Link mitosis to identical DNA.

exam.q: Give two advantages of using tissue culture in plant breeding programmes.
model: Large numbers of plants produced quickly.
Plants are genetically identical so all have the desired characteristics / can be done all year round / in little space / disease-free plants / conserve rare species.
exam.tip: Any two different valid advantages.

exam.q: Give one disadvantage of growing a whole crop from tissue culture.
model: No genetic variation so all plants susceptible to the same disease / pest.
exam.tip: Mention the consequence (disease could wipe out the crop).

exam.q: Explain how tissue culture can be useful in medical research.
model: Cells / tissues can be grown to test new drugs.
To see if drugs are toxic / effective before trials on animals or humans.
Fewer animals need to be used.
Cells are genetically identical so results are valid / differences are due to the drug, not genetics.
Allows study of how diseases such as cancer develop.
exam.tip: Four separate points; include the genetically identical / fair test idea.

exam.q: A grower wants to produce 10 000 orchid plants of a rare variety that has very few seeds. Explain why tissue culture is a better method than growing from seed.
model: Very many plants can be produced from a small amount of tissue.
Production is quick / all year round.
Plants are genetically identical so all have the rare variety's characteristics.
Seeds would show variation because of sexual reproduction, so characteristics could be lost.
Few seeds are produced so seed-growing would not give enough plants.
exam.tip: Apply your answer to orchids and rare / few seeds.

exam.q: Describe how a gardener could use tissue culture to produce many plants from one plant with desirable characteristics.
model: Select a parent plant with the desired characteristics.
Cut small pieces of tissue (explants), for example from the shoot tip / meristem.
Sterilise the explants / use aseptic technique to kill microorganisms.
Place on agar / growth medium containing nutrients (glucose, mineral ions).
Add plant hormones (auxins / cytokinins) to stimulate cell division.
Cells divide by mitosis to form a callus of undifferentiated cells.
Change hormone balance so that roots and shoots develop.
Transfer plantlets to compost / greenhouse to grow.
exam.tip: Write in order with linking words (first, then, next). Six correct, ordered points with a reason or two gets full marks.

exam.q: Evaluate the use of tissue culture to produce all the banana plants for a large plantation.
model: Advantage: many plants produced quickly.
Advantage: all genetically identical so uniform fruit with desirable characteristics, easier to harvest and sell.
Advantage: can produce disease-free plants from meristem tissue.
Disadvantage: no genetic variation so a single disease / pest could destroy the whole plantation.
Disadvantage: expensive / needs skilled workers and lab.
Disadvantage: risk of contamination of cultures.
Conclusion: e.g. beneficial for yield, but risky unless other varieties are also grown to keep variation.
exam.tip: Balanced answer plus a justified conclusion is needed for top band.

worked.q: One explant produces a callus that is divided into 4 every 4 weeks. Each piece then produces a new callus of the same size. Starting from 1 explant, how many cultures are there after 16 weeks?
steps: 16 weeks / 4 weeks = 4 rounds of division.
Each round multiplies the number by 4.
Number = 1 x 4 x 4 x 4 x 4 = 4^4.
worked.ans: 256 cultures, all genetically identical, showing why tissue culture produces large numbers quickly.

worked.q: A scientist tests a new drug on cultured human liver cells. Explain two reasons why using tissue culture improves this investigation.
steps: Reason 1: all the cells are genetically identical (made by mitosis).
So any difference between treated cells and control cells is caused by the drug, not by genetic differences, making it a fair, valid test.
Reason 2: large numbers of cells can be grown.
So the test can be repeated many times to check results are repeatable, without using animals.
worked.ans: Identical cells control genetic variables (valid results) and large numbers allow repeats while reducing animal use.

worked.q: A farmer grows a field of strawberry plants all produced by tissue culture. A new fungal disease arrives. Predict and explain what will happen.
steps: The plants are all clones, so they have the same alleles.
If one plant has no resistance to the fungus, none of them do.
The disease spreads through the field and affects every plant.
In a crop grown from seed, some plants might carry alleles giving resistance and survive.
worked.ans: The whole crop is likely to be damaged or destroyed, because tissue culture gives no genetic variation.

bio_edx.3.8.summary: **Genetic engineering** is the process of **modifying the genome** of an organism to introduce **desirable characteristics**, usually by inserting a gene from another organism. A **restriction enzyme** cuts the gene out of the donor DNA and cuts open a **vector** (such as a bacterial **plasmid** or a **virus**), leaving matching **sticky ends**. **DNA ligase** joins the gene into the vector to make **recombinant DNA**, and the vector carries the gene into the host cell, which then makes the new protein, for example **human insulin** made by bacteria.

core.p: Every organism's **genome** is its entire set of DNA. Genetic engineering changes this genome directly, by adding a gene (or sometimes removing or changing one), so the organism gains a characteristic it did not have before. Because the **genetic code is universal** (the same base triplets code for the same amino acids in all organisms), a human gene can be read by a bacterium and used to make the same human protein.
bullets: Spec 4.10: genetic engineering is a process which involves **modifying the genome** of an organism to introduce **desirable characteristics**.
The new organism is called a **genetically modified (GM) organism**; if it contains a gene from another species it is **transgenic**.
Different from selective breeding: genetic engineering is **faster**, more **precise** (one gene) and can move genes **between species**.
Examples: bacteria making **human insulin**; crops given genes for herbicide or insect resistance; Golden Rice containing genes to make **beta-carotene** (used to make vitamin A).

callouts.p: A process which involves modifying the genome of an organism to introduce desirable characteristics.
DNA has the same structure and the genetic code is the same in all organisms, so a gene from one species can be expressed in another.

core.h: The four tools you must name
core.p: Spec 4.11 asks you to describe the main stages of genetic engineering including the use of **restriction enzymes, ligase, sticky ends and vectors**. Learn what each one is and what it does.
bullets: **Restriction enzymes** cut DNA at specific base sequences.
**Sticky ends** are the short single-stranded overhangs of unpaired bases left by a staggered cut.
**Ligase** is an enzyme that joins pieces of DNA together.
**Vectors** carry the gene into the host cell (plasmids or viruses).

core.p: Restriction enzymes come naturally from bacteria (where they cut up the DNA of invading viruses). Each restriction enzyme recognises one particular short **base sequence**, called a **recognition site**, and cuts the DNA there. Because enzymes are **specific**, only the matching sequence fits the enzyme's active site.
bullets: The recognition site is usually 4 to 8 base pairs long; for example the enzyme EcoRI recognises **GAATTC**.
Many restriction enzymes make a **staggered cut**: the two DNA strands are cut at slightly different points.
This leaves short single-stranded sections of **unpaired bases**: the **sticky ends**.
The **same restriction enzyme** is used to cut both the donor DNA (to remove the gene) and the vector (to open it up).

callouts.p: An enzyme that cuts DNA at a specific base sequence, often leaving sticky ends.

core.p: Sticky ends are the key to joining DNA from two different sources. They are called sticky because their unpaired bases can form **hydrogen bonds** with **complementary** unpaired bases on another sticky end (A pairs with T, C pairs with G).
bullets: When the **same** restriction enzyme cuts both the gene and the plasmid, they have **complementary sticky ends**.
The sticky ends of the gene **base pair** with the sticky ends of the opened plasmid.
This holds the gene in the correct place in the plasmid until ligase seals it.
If **different** restriction enzymes were used, the sticky ends would not match and could not pair.

callouts.p: Short lengths of single-stranded DNA with unpaired bases, produced by a staggered cut, that can join to complementary sticky ends.
Sticky ends do not stick by themselves permanently. Complementary base pairing holds them temporarily; ligase forms the permanent bonds in the backbone.

core.p: Once the sticky ends have paired, there are still gaps in the **sugar-phosphate backbone** of each strand. **DNA ligase** is an enzyme that joins these gaps, permanently joining the gene into the vector.
bullets: Ligase joins the **sugar-phosphate backbones** of the two pieces of DNA.
The result is a single continuous DNA molecule containing DNA from two sources: **recombinant DNA**.
A plasmid that now contains the new gene is called a **recombinant plasmid**.
Ligase is an enzyme, so it works best at its optimum temperature and pH.

core.p: A **vector** is something used to carry the new gene into the host cell. The two vectors named in GCSE are **plasmids** and **viruses**.
bullets: **Plasmids** are small, circular rings of DNA found in bacteria, separate from the main bacterial chromosome. They can be taken up by bacteria and are copied when the bacterium divides.
**Viruses** naturally inject their DNA into host cells, so a virus can be engineered to carry a useful gene into a cell (for example a plant or animal cell).
The vector is cut with the restriction enzyme, the gene is inserted, and ligase seals it.
The recombinant vector is then put into the **host cell** (for example a bacterium).

core.h: The main stages of genetic engineering, in order
core.p: Use this order for any 'describe the stages' question. The example used most often is making **human insulin** using bacteria.
bullets: **1. Identify and isolate** the desired gene (for example the human insulin gene) from the donor DNA.
**2. Cut out the gene** using a **restriction enzyme**, leaving **sticky ends**.
**3. Cut open the vector** (a plasmid) with the **same restriction enzyme**, so it has **complementary sticky ends**.
**4. Mix** the gene and the cut plasmid: the sticky ends pair by complementary base pairing.
**5. DNA ligase** joins the gene into the plasmid, forming a **recombinant plasmid**.
**6. Insert** the recombinant plasmid into a **host cell** (a bacterium).
**7.** The bacteria **reproduce** rapidly (binary fission) in a fermenter; each new bacterium contains the gene.
**8.** The gene is **expressed**: the bacteria make the protein (insulin), which is **extracted and purified**.

core.p: People with **type 1 diabetes** cannot make enough insulin and need injections. Insulin used to be extracted from the pancreases of pigs and cattle. Genetic engineering now lets bacteria make **human insulin** in huge fermenters.
bullets: Large amounts can be made **quickly** and **cheaply**, because bacteria reproduce very fast.
It is **identical to human insulin**, so it is less likely to cause an **allergic reaction** than animal insulin.
No animals are needed, which avoids **ethical** and **religious** objections.
Supply is reliable and not limited by the number of animals slaughtered.

callouts.p: Bacteria reproduce rapidly, are easy to grow in fermenters, have plasmids that are easy to modify, and every new bacterium copies the plasmid, so all offspring make insulin.

core.p: The same stages are used to modify plants and animals, though the host cells are different.
bullets: **Herbicide-resistant crops**: crops given a gene so they survive weedkiller sprayed on the field.
**Insect-resistant (Bt) crops**: given a gene from the bacterium Bacillus thuringiensis to make a toxin that kills insect pests (covered in more detail in 4.12B).
**Golden Rice**: given genes so that the rice grain makes **beta-carotene**, which the body uses to make **vitamin A**.
In plants, genes are often inserted into a few cells, which are then grown into whole plants by **tissue culture**.

core.h: Why the host makes the new protein
core.p: A gene is a section of DNA that codes for a specific protein. Once the gene is inside the host cell, the host's own machinery uses it to make the protein.
bullets: The gene is **transcribed** into mRNA and **translated** by the host's **ribosomes** into a chain of amino acids.
Because the genetic code is **universal**, the bacterium puts the amino acids together in exactly the human order.
When the bacterium divides, the plasmid is **copied**, so all offspring carry the gene.
Thus a population of identical bacteria (a **clone**) all produce the protein.

callouts.p: Gene = DNA that codes for one protein. The base sequence determines the amino acid sequence.

core.p: Exam questions often ask you to compare these two ways of changing organisms.
bullets: Selective breeding only mixes genes **already present** in a species; genetic engineering can add a gene from a **different species**.
Selective breeding takes **many generations**; genetic engineering can give the result in **one generation**.
Genetic engineering transfers a **single specific gene**, whereas selective breeding moves many genes at once, including unwanted ones.

core.p: Most marks are lost by using vague words. Always use the exact names of the enzymes and structures.
bullets: Say '**restriction enzyme**' not 'scissors enzyme' or 'cutting enzyme'.
Say '**ligase**' joins the DNA, not 'glue'.
Say the **same** restriction enzyme cuts both the gene and the plasmid, **so** the sticky ends are **complementary**.
Say the plasmid is the **vector** and the bacterium is the **host**.
Finish with the result: bacteria **multiply** and **produce** the protein.

callouts.p: The plasmid is not the host. The plasmid (vector) carries the gene; the bacterium (host cell) makes the protein.

analogy.t: Cut and paste in a word processor
analogy.p: Genetic engineering is like editing a document. The restriction enzyme is a 'find and cut' tool that only cuts where it finds one exact word (the recognition site). Cutting both documents with the same tool leaves edges that fit together like jigsaw pieces (sticky ends). Ligase is the 'paste and save' that fixes the new paragraph permanently into the document. The vector is the email attachment that carries the edited file into a new computer (the host cell), which then 'runs' the instructions to make the protein. Where it breaks down: in a computer, pasting is exact every time, but in real cells not every plasmid takes up the gene and not every bacterium takes up a plasmid, so scientists must identify which cells were successfully modified.

exam.q: What is meant by genetic engineering?
model: Modifying the genome of an organism to introduce desirable characteristics / inserting a gene from another organism.
exam.tip: Use the word genome or gene.

exam.q: Name the enzyme used to cut DNA at specific base sequences.
model: Restriction enzyme.
exam.tip: 'Restriction' is essential.

exam.q: Name the enzyme used to join a gene into a plasmid.
model: (DNA) ligase.
exam.tip: Spelling must be recognisable.

exam.q: State what is meant by a vector and give one example.
model: Something used to carry / transfer a gene into a (host) cell.
Plasmid / virus.
exam.tip: Two separate marks: meaning and example.

exam.q: Explain why the same restriction enzyme is used to cut the human DNA and the plasmid.
model: So the same / complementary sticky ends are produced.
So the gene and plasmid sticky ends can pair / join (by complementary base pairing).
exam.tip: Mention 'complementary'.

exam.q: Describe what is meant by sticky ends.
model: Short single-stranded sections of DNA / unpaired bases.
Produced when a restriction enzyme makes a staggered cut / can pair with complementary bases.
exam.tip: Say both what they are and how they form or what they do.

exam.q: Give two advantages of producing human insulin using genetically modified bacteria rather than extracting it from animals.
model: Large quantities produced quickly / cheaply.
Identical to human insulin so fewer allergic reactions / no ethical or religious objections to using animals.
exam.tip: Compare with animal insulin.

exam.q: Explain why bacteria are used as host cells for producing human proteins.
model: Bacteria reproduce quickly.
They contain plasmids that can be used as vectors.
The plasmid is copied each time the bacterium divides so all offspring make the protein / genetic code is universal so the human gene is expressed.
exam.tip: Three distinct reasons.

exam.q: Explain the role of DNA ligase in genetic engineering.
model: Joins the gene to the plasmid / vector DNA.
By joining the sugar-phosphate backbone / forms recombinant DNA.
exam.tip: Link to recombinant DNA.

exam.q: Describe how genetic engineering is used to produce bacteria that make human insulin.

Cut out using a restriction enzyme.
Leaving sticky ends.
Plasmid cut open with the same restriction enzyme.
Complementary sticky ends join / base pair.
DNA ligase joins the gene into the plasmid forming a recombinant plasmid.
Plasmid (vector) inserted into a bacterium (host).
Bacteria reproduce / grown in a fermenter and make insulin, which is extracted and purified.
exam.tip: Give stages in order and name all four tools.

exam.q: Golden Rice has been genetically engineered to make beta-carotene in its grains. Suggest how a virus could be used in this process.
model: The beta-carotene gene is inserted into the virus DNA (using restriction enzymes and ligase).
The virus acts as a vector.
The virus infects / injects its DNA into rice cells, carrying the gene into them.
exam.tip: Apply the vector idea to an unfamiliar organism.

worked.q: A plasmid is 4400 base pairs long. A restriction enzyme cuts it once. A human gene of 1350 base pairs is inserted. What is the length of the recombinant plasmid?
steps: Cutting a circular plasmid once opens it but does not remove any base pairs.
The gene is inserted into the gap.
= 5750 base pairs.
worked.ans: 5750 base pairs.

worked.q: One genetically modified bacterium divides every 20 minutes. How many bacteria containing the insulin gene are there after 4 hours, assuming all survive?
steps: 4 hours = 240 minutes.
Number of divisions = 240 / 20 = 12.
Each division doubles the number: 2^12.
worked.ans: 4096 bacteria, each with a copy of the recombinant plasmid, because the plasmid is copied every time the bacterium divides.

worked.q: A restriction enzyme recognises GGATCC and cuts between the two G bases. A student cuts the human gene with this enzyme but cuts the plasmid with a different enzyme that recognises GAATTC. Explain why the gene will not be inserted.
steps: The two enzymes recognise different base sequences.
So they leave different sticky ends (GATC overhang vs AATT overhang).
The sticky ends are not complementary, so their bases cannot pair.
Ligase cannot join DNA that is not held together, so no recombinant plasmid forms.
worked.ans: The sticky ends are not complementary, so the gene cannot base pair with and be joined into the plasmid; the same restriction enzyme must be used for both.

bio_edx.3.9.summary: A **genetically modified (GM) organism** has had its genome changed by genetic engineering to give it a **desirable characteristic**. The key GCSE example is **insect-resistant (Bt) crops**, given a gene from the bacterium **Bacillus thuringiensis** so their cells make a **Bt toxin** that kills insect larvae which eat them. This raises **yields** and cuts **insecticide** use, but insects may **evolve resistance**, the gene may **spread to wild plants**, and there are worries about **biodiversity**, cost and long-term effects, so GM organisms must be **evaluated** by weighing benefits against risks.

core.p: A GM organism is any organism whose **genome** has been altered using genetic engineering. Usually a gene from another species is inserted (so it is also **transgenic**). The gene is cut out with restriction enzymes, joined into a vector with ligase, and transferred into the host's cells. The organism then makes a new protein that gives it a useful characteristic.
bullets: This is a **triple only (B)** point: you must be able to **evaluate** the advantages and disadvantages.
GM **crop plants**: insect resistance (Bt), herbicide resistance, Golden Rice (beta-carotene), drought or disease resistance.
GM **microorganisms**: bacteria that make human insulin.
GM **animals** are also produced, for example for medical research or to make useful proteins.
Most GM plants are made by inserting the gene into a few plant cells and growing them into whole plants using **tissue culture**.

callouts.p: An organism whose genome has been modified by genetic engineering to introduce desirable characteristics.

core.h: Insect-resistant Bt crops: how they are made
core.p: **Bacillus thuringiensis** is a soil bacterium that naturally makes a protein toxin (**Bt toxin**) that kills the larvae (caterpillars) of certain insects. The gene for this toxin is transferred into crop plants such as maize (corn), cotton and soya.
bullets: The **Bt toxin gene** is cut out of the bacterial DNA using a **restriction enzyme**.
It is inserted into a **vector** (for example a plasmid of a bacterium that infects plants) with **ligase**.
The vector transfers the gene into **plant cells**.
The modified cells are grown into whole plants by **tissue culture**.
Every cell of the new plant contains the gene and makes **Bt toxin**.

callouts.p: The insect-resistance gene comes from the bacterium Bacillus thuringiensis, so Bt crops are transgenic.

core.p: When an insect larva eats part of a Bt plant, it swallows the Bt toxin. The toxin damages the larva's gut, so it stops feeding and dies. Insects that do not eat the crop are not affected, because the toxin is only inside the plant.
bullets: The toxin is **specific**: it only harms certain insect groups that have the right receptors in their gut.
It is **harmless to humans and other mammals**, which do not have these receptors.
The plant is protected **all the time**, in every part, without spraying.
Less of the crop is eaten, so more is harvested: **higher yield**.

callouts.p: Gene inserted -> plant makes Bt toxin -> insects that eat it die -> less crop damage -> higher yield. Each arrow can be a mark.

core.p: These are the points that mark schemes credit. Always explain WHY each is an advantage.
bullets: **Higher yield**: less crop is lost to insects, so more food is produced per hectare, helping to **feed a growing human population**.
**Less insecticide needs to be sprayed**: this saves money, fuel and labour for farmers.
Fewer insecticides means **less harm to non-target insects** (for example bees and other pollinators) and to the food chains that depend on them.
Fewer insecticides means less risk of chemicals **washing into rivers** or harming **farm workers**.
Only insects that **eat the crop** are killed, whereas sprayed insecticide can kill all insects in the field.
Insecticide sprays can be washed off by rain; the Bt toxin is always inside the plant.

callouts.p: Increased yield and reduced use of insecticide sprays.

core.h: Disadvantages and risks of insect-resistant crops
core.p: Exam questions expect you to know the risks as well as the benefits, and to explain them using biology.
bullets: **Insects may evolve resistance** to Bt toxin by natural selection, so the crop would no longer be protected.
**Non-target insects** that eat pollen or leaves, such as some butterfly larvae, could be harmed, reducing **biodiversity**.
Fewer insects means less food for **insect-eating birds** and other animals in the **food chain**.
The Bt gene might **transfer to wild plants** (for example by cross-pollination with wild relatives), producing insect-resistant weeds.
**GM seed is expensive** and farmers often have to buy new seed each year; this can be hard for farmers in poorer countries.
Some people worry about **unknown long-term effects** on human health or ecosystems.
Growing large areas of one GM crop (a **monoculture**) reduces genetic variation and habitat variety.

callouts.p: Do not just write 'it might be dangerous'. Say exactly what could happen: e.g. 'the gene could spread to wild plants by pollen'.

core.h: How insects evolve resistance to Bt toxin
core.p: This links GM crops to **natural selection** (Topic 4.2) and to antibiotic resistance (4.3). It is a favourite 4 to 6 mark question.
bullets: In the insect population there is **variation**; a **random mutation** may give a few insects an allele for **resistance** to Bt toxin.
When they feed on Bt crops, non-resistant insects die, but resistant insects **survive**.
The resistant insects **reproduce** and pass on the resistance allele to their offspring.
Over many generations, the **frequency of the resistance allele increases**, so most of the population becomes resistant.
Farmers reduce this risk by planting **refuges** of non-GM crop nearby, so non-resistant insects survive and breed with any resistant ones.

callouts.p: The Bt toxin does not cause the mutation. The mutation is already there by chance; the toxin only selects which insects survive.

core.h: Other GM crops you should be able to evaluate
core.p: The same style of evaluation applies to other GM plants. Questions may give you information about an unfamiliar GM organism and ask you to evaluate it.
bullets: **Herbicide-resistant crops**: the crop survives weedkiller, so farmers can spray to kill **weeds** without killing the crop, reducing competition for light, water and minerals and increasing yield. Risks: overuse of herbicide, herbicide-resistant weeds, fewer wild flowers so lower biodiversity.

**Golden Rice**: makes **beta-carotene**, which the body converts to **vitamin A**, helping to prevent vitamin A deficiency (which can cause blindness) in countries where rice is the main food. Concerns: cost, acceptance by farmers, long-term effects.
Crops engineered for **drought or salt tolerance**, **disease resistance** or a longer **shelf life**.

core.p: Not all GM organisms are crops. Genetically modified **bacteria** are used to produce human proteins.
bullets: Bacteria with the human **insulin** gene make insulin for people with **type 1 diabetes**.
Advantages: large amounts made quickly and cheaply; identical to human insulin so fewer allergic reactions; no need to use animals.
Disadvantages: expensive to set up; bacteria must be kept in sterile fermenters; some people have ethical concerns about genetic engineering in general.

core.h: Wider ethical, economic and social issues
core.p: Many evaluation marks come from showing you understand that people disagree about GM organisms for reasons that are not only scientific.
bullets: **Feeding the world**: GM crops could help produce enough food for a growing human population.
**Economic**: large companies own patents on GM seeds; farmers may become dependent on them and pay more for seed.
**Ethical**: some people think it is wrong to move genes between species or 'play God'.
**Consumer choice**: some people do not want to eat GM food; labelling allows choice.
**Uncertainty**: GM crops have been eaten for decades, but long-term effects on ecosystems still need monitoring.

callouts.p: Advantage + reason, disadvantage + reason (at least two of each), then a conclusion that weighs them up, e.g. 'Overall the benefits outweigh the risks if refuges are used to slow resistance'.

core.h: GM crops compared with other ways of controlling pests
core.p: You may be asked to compare GM crops with insecticides or biological control (4.13B).
bullets: **Chemical insecticides**: fast acting but kill useful insects too, can wash into water, need repeated spraying, and pests can evolve resistance.
**Biological control**: uses a natural predator or parasite of the pest; no chemicals, but the control organism could become a pest itself.
**Bt crops**: built-in protection, only affects insects that eat the crop, but resistance can evolve and genes may spread.

core.p: Questions are often based on data (for example yields or insecticide use) or on an unfamiliar GM organism. Read the information carefully and use it.
bullets: Quote numbers from graphs or tables to support each advantage or disadvantage.
Use key terms: **Bt toxin, Bacillus thuringiensis, yield, insecticide, natural selection, resistance, biodiversity, cross-pollination**.
For 'evaluate', always finish with a **justified conclusion**.
For calculations, percentage change = (new - original) / original x 100.

callouts.p: Insect-resistant crops make a toxin that kills insects. Herbicide-resistant crops survive weedkiller. They are different modifications.

analogy.t: A plant with its own built-in bodyguard
analogy.p: A Bt crop is like a house where every room has its own lock built in, instead of paying a security guard (insecticide spray) to patrol the whole street and scare away everyone, including the friendly neighbours (bees). Only someone who tries to break in (eats the plant) is stopped. Where it breaks down: burglars can't change their bodies, but over many generations insect populations can evolve resistance by natural selection, so the lock can stop working; and the 'lock' gene can spread by pollen to wild plants, which a real lock cannot do.

terms.d: An organism whose genome has been altered by genetic engineering to introduce a desirable characteristic.
An organism containing a gene from a different species.
A soil bacterium that produces a toxin that kills certain insect larvae; the source of the Bt gene.
A protein made by Bacillus thuringiensis (and Bt crops) that kills insect larvae that eat it.
A GM crop that produces Bt toxin so insects that eat it die.
A GM crop that is not killed by a particular weedkiller.
A chemical that kills insects.
A chemical that kills plants (weeds).
The amount of crop produced, usually per unit area.
The ability of an organism to survive a substance (e.g. Bt toxin) that would normally kill it.
Individuals with alleles that make them better adapted survive and reproduce, passing on those alleles, so the alleles become more common.
A random change in the base sequence of DNA, which can produce a new allele.
The variety of different species (and genetic variation) in an area.
Transfer of pollen from one plant to another plant; could spread a GM gene to wild relatives.
An area of non-GM crop planted near a Bt crop to slow the evolution of resistance in insect pests.
GM rice that makes beta-carotene, which the body converts to vitamin A.

mistakes.w: Bt crops are sprayed with Bt toxin.
mistakes.r: Bt crops make Bt toxin themselves in their cells because they contain the Bt gene.

mistakes.w: The Bt toxin causes insects to mutate and become resistant.
mistakes.r: Resistance comes from a random mutation already present; the toxin selects resistant insects, which survive and reproduce.

mistakes.w: Insects become resistant during their lifetime.
mistakes.r: The population evolves resistance over many generations as the resistance allele becomes more common.

mistakes.w: GM crops kill all insects.
mistakes.r: Bt toxin only kills insects that eat the crop (and only certain types), unlike sprayed insecticides.

mistakes.w: GM crops use more pesticides.
mistakes.r: Insect-resistant crops need less insecticide to be sprayed.

mistakes.w: Insect-resistant crops let farmers spray weedkiller.
mistakes.r: That is herbicide resistance; insect resistance means the crop makes a toxin against insect pests.

mistakes.w: A disadvantage is that GM crops are unhealthy.
mistakes.r: Give a specific risk: e.g. unknown long-term effects, gene transfer to wild plants, harm to non-target insects, resistance.

mistakes.w: Genes spread to other plants through the soil.
mistakes.r: Genes can spread to wild relatives by pollen (cross-pollination).

mistakes.w: GM crops are always cheaper for farmers.
mistakes.r: Seeds are often more expensive, though money is saved on insecticide.

exam.q: Name the bacterium that is the source of the gene used in insect-resistant crops.
model: Bacillus thuringiensis.
exam.tip: Spelling need only be recognisable; 'Bt' alone may not be enough.

exam.q: Explain how a crop plant containing the Bt gene is protected from insects.
model: The plant makes Bt toxin.
Insects / larvae that eat the plant are killed.
exam.tip: Say the plant MAKES the toxin.

exam.q: Give two advantages to a farmer of growing insect-resistant crops.
model: Higher yield / less crop damage.
Less insecticide needed so lower costs / less labour.
exam.tip: Two different advantages.

exam.q: Give two environmental advantages of growing insect-resistant crops.
model: Less insecticide sprayed, so less harm to non-target insects such as bees.
Less insecticide washing into rivers / less pollution.
exam.tip: Focus on the environment, not money.

exam.q: Suggest why some people are concerned about growing insect-resistant crops.
model: Gene may transfer to wild plants (by pollen).
Insects may evolve resistance / harm non-target insects / unknown long-term effects / reduce biodiversity.
exam.tip: Give specific concerns.

exam.q: Explain how a population of insects could become resistant to the Bt toxin.
model: Random mutation gives some insects an allele for resistance.
Resistant insects survive when they eat the Bt crop; non-resistant insects die.
Resistant insects reproduce, passing on the resistance allele.
Over many generations the allele becomes more frequent in the population.
exam.tip: Natural selection in four steps.

exam.q: Before growing Bt cotton, a farmer sprayed 12 kg of insecticide per hectare. After switching, this fell to 3 kg per hectare. Calculate the percentage decrease.
exam.tip: Divide by the original value.

exam.q: Suggest why farmers growing Bt crops are advised to plant an area of non-GM crops nearby.
model: Non-resistant insects survive in the non-GM area.
They breed with any resistant insects, so the resistance allele stays rare / slows evolution of resistance.
exam.tip: Link to natural selection.

exam.q: Explain why herbicide-resistant crops can increase yield.
model: Farmers can spray herbicide to kill weeds without killing the crop.
Fewer weeds means less competition.
For light, water and mineral ions, so the crop grows better.
exam.tip: Name what plants compete for.

exam.q: Evaluate the use of insect-resistant GM crops to increase food production.
model: Advantage: higher yields, helping to feed a growing population.
Advantage: less insecticide sprayed, saving money and reducing harm to other insects and pollution.
Advantage: only insects that eat the crop are killed.
Disadvantage: insects may evolve resistance by natural selection.
Disadvantage: gene may spread to wild plants by cross-pollination / harm to non-target species / reduced biodiversity.
Disadvantage: expensive seeds / unknown long-term effects / ethical objections.
Justified conclusion, e.g. benefits outweigh risks if refuges are used and effects are monitored.
exam.tip: Balanced points plus a conclusion for the top band.

worked.q: A field of normal maize produced 6.4 tonnes per hectare. The same field with Bt maize produced 8.0 tonnes per hectare. Calculate the percentage increase in yield.
steps: Increase = 8.0 - 6.4 = 1.6 tonnes per hectare.
Percentage increase = increase / original x 100.
worked.ans: 25% increase in yield.

worked.q: Model answer: Explain two possible effects of growing large areas of Bt crops on a food chain that includes insect-eating birds.
steps: Bt crops kill the insect larvae that eat them, so the number of these insects falls.
Insect-eating birds then have less food, so their population may decrease.
However, less insecticide is sprayed, so fewer non-target insects (that do not eat the crop) are killed.
This could leave more of those insects as food for birds than if the field were sprayed.
worked.ans: Fewer crop-eating insects may mean less food for birds, but reduced spraying may protect other insects, so the overall effect depends on which insects the birds eat.

worked.q: Applied example: A company develops GM potatoes resistant to a fungal disease. Evaluate whether a poor farming region should grow them.
steps: Advantage: less crop lost to disease, so higher yield and more food.
Advantage: less fungicide needed, saving money and reducing pollution.
Disadvantage: GM seed may be expensive and may need to be bought each year.
Disadvantage: the fungus may evolve to overcome resistance; all plants are genetically similar so one new strain could affect all of them.
Conclusion: weigh up the food security benefit against cost and long-term risk.
worked.ans: Likely beneficial for food supply if seed is affordable, but the region should keep other varieties to reduce the risk of the fungus evolving and to maintain genetic variation.
